lede: 130 decisions for turning the Alftian Codex, the Necrocursica and the Corrant Papers into current canon, with Kwon Mu-jin writing the Codex, Malphas writing the Necrocursica and a new author writing the Papers. A nine-part audit checked every point where the texts meet the Fracture of Worlds system, and a second agent checked each finding. Only the choices that are yours are here. The 109 fixes where canon already decides are listed at the end.
fixesIntro: Canon already decides each of these, so I'll make them without asking. Those marked 'after' wait on a question above. The conflict rows get recorded, not resolved. Flag anything here you disagree with in the box under each group.

sections.title: Keystones
sections.intro: Answer these first. Every later section leans on at least one of them.

questions.title: Which era the texts are dated in
questions.question: The texts stamp themselves 'Era of Voyagers' (Imperial years 0 to 70); how should they be dated now that their authors live in Year 715?
questions.context: The Codex's colophons (closing notes on where a copy was made), the Papers' sign-off and some prose lines place the texts in the 'Era of Voyagers'. Canon's Voyager Era is Imperial years 0 to 70, whose first decades 'built nothing'. Rail runs on the mains (Essence conduits), laid from about 315 IC, so trains fit the Withering Era (645 to now), not the Voyager Era. The Errata (a Guild correction notice) says of the Alftian codices 'not one of them cites an Age'. The Necrocursica has no stamp.

options.label: Re-stamp everything 'Withering Era' with an Imperial year
options.consequence: About a dozen stamps and prose lines change across the Codex volumes, the Papers and the Codex wiki pages, each given a year near 700 IC. The Errata's line that the codices cite no Age is rewritten, an edit to a Guild canon instrument.

options.label: No Age stamp; dates follow from the authors' own lives
options.consequence: Every 'Era of Voyagers' is cut, from colophons and prose alike. Colophons keep archive and place; dates are the authors' own ('my thirtieth year', 'six years after the letter'). Rail places the texts in the present, and the Errata stands as written.

options.label: Archive shelf-stamp says Withering Era; authors' text cites no Age
options.consequence: Only the archive transcription notes (the Silent Archivists', the Urbis Archivum's) carry a Withering-Era year. The authors' prose never names an Age, and the Errata gains one line saying it means the authors' own text.

questions.rec_reason: It agrees with the Errata word for word and edits no canon, and 'Era of Voyagers' is not even canon's spelling. The trains already place the texts in the present; Mu-jin's and Malphas's own years date the events.
questions.evidence: Concordance of Ages 110-113, 130; Four Ceilings 155, 241, 275; Mechanica 65; Errata 39; Volume the First 14; Vol II docx 5, 281; Vol III docx 406; Papers 286

questions.title: Is the Heresiology written after the texts?
questions.question: The Heresiology's five Historical Cases are the Codex's own events; is it written after all five texts, or are its cases older incidents that merely resemble them?
questions.context: The Heresiology of Alchemy (the Accord's manual on corrupt alchemy) teaches from five cases: a king sealed against contradiction, a compelled author's necromantic manuscript, an eastern commission that rebuilt a dead woman, the Genesio activations and the drift of Tempus (a body in the sky). These are the Codex's events. The Codex meta page calls the Heresiology 'the finished version of a book this man left open'; Malphas's card says it 'named him without naming him'. It is undated, and Mu-jin is 38.

options.label: After: a recent Accord manual drawn from these events
options.consequence: The five cases stand word for word; the meta page and Malphas's card stay true. The texts' events close some years before its issue, in Mu-jin's past. Case II's author 'pulled by access and manipulated through need' must fit Malphas (the Necrocursica items).

options.label: Before: its cases are older incidents that only resemble these
options.consequence: Cases I to V are reworded so they stop matching (no Genesio, no Tempus, no eastern commission). The meta page's 'finished version' line is cut, and Volume II's coining of the Corruption names becomes a quotation of the Heresiology.

options.label: After, and Mu-jin himself finishes it
options.consequence: Mu-jin, an Archmagus of the Accord's Division of Alchemetrica, writes the manual that closes his open book. His card gains the work, and the Heresiology gains a note tracing it to his unfinished fourth volume, while its voice must still read as the Accord's.

questions.rec_reason: The cases match the texts too closely to be coincidence, and this edits no canon: the cases, the meta page and Malphas's card all read true as written. The Accord finishing Mu-jin's open book keeps the manual institutional.
questions.evidence: Heresiology 11-15 (undated header), 206-212 (Cases I-V); Alftian Codex meta page 64; Malphas's card 45, 142; Mu-jin's card 26; Vol I docx 130; Vol II docx 27, 85

questions.title: When in his life each volume falls
questions.question: When in Mu-jin's life do the Codex's events happen, and when does he write each of the three volumes?
questions.context: Vol I looks back; Vol II is a working journal; Vol III follows 'eleven months' in Urbis and says Gillus has corresponded 'through your own text for six years', so Vols I–II circulated six or more years earlier. Canon, as the Academy pages read R57-01: left court at fourteen; road years with Ara; Rimward (right eye lost) and the Ashgate road (one lung left) at 24; the Academy at 38, today. The Heresiology (the treatise on alchemy's corruptions) holds Vol III's Genesio events as Case IV, so they predate today.

options.label: All three volumes in the road years, before Rimward
options.consequence: Vols I–II by about eighteen, Vol III by 24, his body whole throughout, the Codex squeezed into ten years beside his school. The Correction (Vol III's thesis) predates Rimward, so Rimward tests the doctrine instead of prompting it.

options.label: Vols I–II on the road; Vol III after the Ashgate road
options.consequence: Vols I–II fall between fourteen and about nineteen; the eleven months in Urbis become his convalescence on one lung, before the Academy. The Correction answers Rimward. 'Final Testimonies' and 'life's work' go, and Vol III must mention Frithia and infant children.

options.label: Vols I–II on the road; Vol III written now, at the Academy
options.consequence: Vol III becomes a teacher's recollection of Genesio, its present tense turned past. 'Final' fits, but eleven months in Urbis collide with his homeroom, and a Heresiology drawn from Vol III could not yet exist, though cards cite it.

questions.rec_reason: Only B fits the six-year gap, gives the eleven months a cause, and lets the Correction be the shape he promised Ara after Rimward. Vol III's events still fall before today, as the Heresiology and the Malphas card require.
questions.evidence: Vol III docx:5, :16, :66, :402; Mu-jin card:147, :176-185; Vaeloris:1872-1880; Academy State of Play:13; Night Watch bible:151; Heresiology:208-212; Malphas card:45

questions.title: Texts' doctrine: system canon or one school's reading
questions.question: Do the residues, the Volitional Trace and impression-bodies become facts on the system pages, or stay what the Accord teaches inside the story?
questions.context: The Codex meta page says the Codex 'establishes' a fourth residue, the Volitional Trace (the record of a decision someone died in the middle of), 'entered into the formal canon' by the narrator's testimony. The Heresiology already treats impression-bodies (likenesses rebuilt from a dead person's residue) as real. Rule R47-12 keeps unknowns open: any answer is one school's reading. The texts disagree: Gillus's letter calls the Trace a record, 'Not the person'; the Necrocursica says it 'retains agency' and keeps pursuing its decision.

options.label: System canon: residues, Trace and impression-bodies all become fact
options.consequence: The Lexicon, The Crossing and the Magical Categories gain entries, and the Heresiology must agree line for line. The Trace's behaviour, whichever reading wins, becomes a rule every scene obeys.

options.label: In-world doctrine only: the Accord's school reading
options.consequence: System pages record the whole scheme as the Accord's teaching and leave it open under R47-12. Least canon churn; the death-seam mapping questions become questions about what the school claims.

options.label: Mixed: residues and impression-bodies canon, the Trace contested
options.consequence: The Crossing and the Lexicon gain the residues and impression-bodies. The Trace is the Accord's reading, resting on Mu-jin's testimony through his Anamnesis (memory-current) read of unfinished intention, beside the rival readings (record or agent): a mystery players can investigate.

questions.rec_reason: The Heresiology already makes impression-bodies real, so they are canon either way. A finding resting on one man's testimony, with the texts split on whether it acts, is exactly the open, findable mystery R47-12 and fair play want.
questions.evidence: Alftian Codex meta page 59, 63; Heresiology 66, 170; R47-12; Papers 251 ('Not the person'); Necrocursica 109 ('retains agency'); Mu-jin's card 48 (Anamnesis)

questions.title: Sublimatio or Sublimare: which one is sublimation
questions.question: Which twin current is sublimation (a solid turning straight to vapour) and which is fractional distillation (separating a mixture by boiling off its parts)?
questions.context: Vectoria's page and the Eight Families give Sublimatio the sublimation analogue and Sublimare fractional distillation. Alchemetrica says the opposite: Sublimare 'elevates without passing through the states between' and the Sublimation operation mirrors it, as do rule R18-5 and Kytheris's card. Malphas's Necrocursica follows the physics ('Sublimatio elevates without intermediate states') but later calls a separating cleanse of the Aether Shell 'Sublimatio-aligned'. The answer decides whether the Distillation stage already has a current among the Sixty.

options.label: The physics register wins
options.consequence: Sublimatio is sublimation, Sublimare is distillation. Alchemetrica's operation table, R18-5's list and Kytheris's card are corrected, and Distillation mirrors Sublimare. The Necrocursica's Sublimatio line stands; its separating cleanse becomes Sublimare-aligned.

options.label: Alchemetrica wins
options.consequence: Sublimare is sublimation. Vectoria's analogues and failure modes swap between the twins, the Necrocursica's Sublimatio line becomes Sublimare, and Distillation has no current among the Sixty unless K6 admits one.

questions.rec_reason: The physics register gives each twin a physical analogue and a failure mode, the Eight Families already records the split and leans physical, and Distillation gains a home without a new Wellspring.
questions.evidence: Vectoria 42, 49; Eight Families 194; Alchemetrica 30, 103, 119; R18-5 (pack 18, 268-280); Kytheris card 17; Necrocursica 81, 233

questions.title: Calcination and Distillation: Wellsprings or bench operations
questions.question: Are Calcination and Distillation Wellsprings (currents a soul can tune to), folk names for two of the Sixty, or only procedures done at the bench?
questions.context: Rule R18-5 (ratified 09-12) and Alchemetrica name eight Wellsprings that are also alchemical operations, Calcination and Distillation among them; the Necrocursica counts Calcination among 'the sixty'. The Lists sheet (the Master Codex register) and Fracture of Worlds hold exactly sixty, neither name among them, and R18-2, same day, takes Wellspring names only from that sheet. Mu-jin's card lists 'Calcination' and 'Distillatio'. Near matches exist: Cinerion (heat Family: 'what survives a fire is not waste') and Sublimare (mechanics Family, analogue: fractional distillation).

options.label: Bench operations only; the Sixty stay untouched
options.consequence: A logged ruling amends R18-5, and Alchemetrica's 'eight' table drops to six. Mu-jin's card loses two harmonisations, and about ten pages (Ossuary Choir, Ignatius, Vaelen, Vorynth, The Open Crucible, Spirit Rune Arts) are re-pointed to real currents.

options.label: Alchemists' folk names for Cinerion and Sublimare
options.consequence: Cinerion's page records 'Calcination', Sublimare's 'Distillation' and 'Distillatio', as folk names (R50-25). Alchemetrica's phase-skipping row moves from Sublimare to Sublimatio, so all eight are in the Sixty. R18-5 and the cards stand; Calcination keeps the cards' Caloria (heat) Family.

options.label: Admit both as new Wellsprings, making sixty-two
options.consequence: 'The Sixty' breaks in Fracture of Worlds, the Lists sheet and every Family count. It needs a demonstrated-absence proposal under R18-2 and a ruling past R5-A, which keeps the skeleton unchanged.

questions.rec_reason: The only option that keeps both 09-12 ratifications true: every Wellspring still comes from the Lists sheet (R18-2) and both names stay Wellsprings (R18-5). Each gains a real current, the alchemy-to-magic tie this rewrite is for.
questions.evidence: Lists sheet rows 2-61; Fracture of Worlds V 29-128; Alchemetrica 23-35, 102-103; R18-2; R18-5; R50-25; Caloria (Cinerion); Vectoria (Sublimare); Mu-jin's card 48; Necrocursica 81, 213

questions.title: Which residue list the texts use
questions.question: What does a dead person leave behind in the converted texts: the Codex's three residues, the Necrocursica's four, both on different clocks, or The Crossing's three products?
questions.context: The Codex, meta page and Papers credit the Necrocursica with three residues: Harmonic Imprint (a place's imprint), Sympathetic Bond Trace (the thread to loved ones) and Parunic Echo (a practitioner's glyph-trace). The Necrocursica lists four: Corporeal Residue (the body), Aetheric Shell (the outer field), Nospheric Echo (the mind's imprint on places) and Volitional Trace. The Crossing (canon) splits the soul into Echo (gone within hours), Temperance Residue (back to the Wellspring in nine days) and Name-record (filed forever). The Codex's grief commission comes two years after the death.

options.label: Both lists on two clocks, hinged on The Crossing's nine days
options.consequence: The Necrocursica's four are the forensic reading inside the nine days; the Codex's three (place, bond, glyph-trace) are what stays after, which the two-year-old commission draws on. The Necrocursica gains a short after-window section, so the Codex and Papers cite it truly.

options.label: The Necrocursica's four; the Codex's three become older names
options.consequence: A mapping line reads the Harmonic Imprint as the Nospheric Echo, the Bond Trace as a relational thread and the Parunic Echo as a working's residue. The Corporeal Residue joins the trade in rendering the dead. The Codex, meta page and two Papers lines change.

options.label: The Crossing's three products, with the Trace a disputed fourth
options.consequence: Tightest fit with canon, but the Temperance Residue is gone by day nine, so the two-year-old commission has nothing to build from, and the Bond Trace that Volume III and the Papers' plot run on disappears. All five texts change.

options.label: The Codex's three plus the Trace
options.consequence: The Codex, meta page and Papers stand. The Necrocursica loses its forensic chapter and its Tria Prima of the dead (the body as Salt, of the alchemists' Sulphur, Salt and Mercury), which must be rebuilt.

questions.rec_reason: Keeps both authors' material, sets each list on The Crossing's clock, and explains why a two-year-old commission has material. The residues are the meta page's 'dents left on the surface beneath', which is why an impression-body is not the person.
questions.evidence: The Crossing 22-59; Vol II docx 89-99, 187; Necrocursica 93-111; Alftian Codex meta page 57-58; Papers 57, 171; Volume the Second 82-84; Standing Index 54-59

questions.title: Which seven keeps 'Seven Cacodaemonic Corruptions'
questions.question: The Heresiology and the Necrocursica give the name 'Seven Cacodaemonic Corruptions' to two different lists; which list keeps it?
questions.context: The Heresiology's Seven Cacodaemonic Corruptions are the seven stages of the Great Work (alchemy's seven-step refinement) turned inside out; its tribunal Grade III (a severity grade) rests on them, and the Codex uses the same list. The Necrocursica's title and chapter 3 give that name to seven Mortalis (death-Wellspring) failures, Mirror Trace to Completion, and call the first four mechanical, not ideological. Canon already calls confusing two sevens 'the standard error'. Volume I uses the name while its author has not read the Necrocursica, whose title carries it.

options.label: Heresiology keeps it; the Necrocursica's become the Seven Unmoorings
options.consequence: The Necrocursica's title, chapter 3 heading and Appendix II are renamed from the text's own verb ('it unmoors them', chapter 4), and each failure may name the Heresiology inversion that drives it. Grade III and the God Hand page's 'two sevens' stay true.

options.label: One seven: nest the Mortalis failures under the Heresiology's inversions
options.consequence: Each failure is rewritten as the death-form of one inversion (Mirror Trace under Dissolution Perverted). A heavy rewrite, and forced for the four failures the Necrocursica itself calls mechanical rather than ideological.

options.label: Both keep it; Malphas takes the name on purpose
options.consequence: Malphas titles his seven as a deliberate answer to the Codex's list, and a gloss says so. Grade III must specify 'the Seven of the Heresiology', and the God Hand page's 'two sevens' note must count three.

questions.rec_reason: Smallest edit, keeps Grade III and the God Hand page true, and respects the Necrocursica's own line that its first four failures are mechanical. 'Unmoorings' comes from the text's own verb.
questions.evidence: Heresiology 23, 57-143, 184; Necrocursica docx 3, 187, 199-339, 285, 421-425; Vol I 162-165; Vol II docx 147; The Crossing and the Making of the God Hand 71-73

questions.title: Base text: full Word files or wiki
questions.question: Which version is the base for the conversion: the full first-person Word files, or the shorter Codex pages on the wiki?
questions.context: All five texts exist as full Word files; Volume I's is in the vault (the attached file was a copy of Volume III). The wiki's Codex pages keep about 60% of the words. They switch narration to third person, drop the colophons, dates, places, travel times and authorship lines (who designed the Trace method, the attribution chain), and turn 'forced' into 'compelled'. They also silently dropped two Stage errors. They are marked unverified, and they look consistent mainly because they cut the lines that conflict.

options.label: Word files as base; wiki condensations regenerated afterwards
options.consequence: Every contradiction is visible and decided here. The converted texts are first person throughout, and the wiki's Codex pages are rewritten afterwards as condensations of the new text, keeping their chapter subheads and residue table.

options.label: Wiki condensation as base
options.consequence: Faster and already shorter, but it inherits the mixed voice, one changed meaning and silence on facts the later texts rely on (Volume III's references to the investigator's notes, the Genesio travel distance, the attribution chain).

options.label: Word files as base; the wiki hosts the full text
options.consequence: As the first option, but the condensed pages are retired and the wiki carries the full converted volumes, so there is one version to keep in step instead of two.

questions.rec_reason: The Word files are the only complete source, and the condensation hides contradictions rather than fixing them. A short wiki page still earns its place as the way into a long text.
questions.evidence: Codex wiki pages keep 58-65% of the Word files' words; Volume the First 8, 86, 156; Vol II docx 67, 149; Vol III docx 66, 340, 404

questions.title: How deep the rewrite goes
questions.question: How deep does the conversion go: surgical edits, a substantial rewrite into the new authors' voices, a full rebuild, or a split by text?
questions.context: The five texts run about 27,000 words of strong prose. Under Mu-jin the Codex narrator's life, origin and the flaw the story turns on change: Vis is an Elfin terrace-farmers' son with three friends and a monastery; Mu-jin is a human Mahuo court prodigy, catalyst at fourteen, who left when the court made him a symbol. Under Malphas the Necrocursica's author changes from a poet writing under compulsion to an expelled Pyraeon Forge alchemist who founds the cult The Mother. The Papers' author is new and has no card.

options.label: Surgical: names, terms, dates and mechanics; the prose stays
options.consequence: Fastest, and the prose survives intact. But Vis's farm childhood, Elfin body and monastery friendships stay on the page under Mu-jin's name, and the Necrocursica's title page keeps Noxinus's confinement and wounded hand under Malphas's.

options.label: Substantial: keep beats and theory, rewrite prose in the new voices
options.consequence: Every chapter's events, arguments and set lines (the Aphorism of Mortalis, the letter, the platform coffee) stay; narration is redrafted from the cards and archived scenes. About 27,000 words redrafted.

options.label: Rebuild: new texts from the same ideas
options.consequence: Structure, events and cast are rethought around the new authors, and the old texts become source notes. Most freedom, but the proven prose goes and the Heresiology's case-by-case match must be rechecked.

options.label: Split: substantial for the Codex and Necrocursica, surgical for the Papers
options.consequence: The two texts whose narrators' lives change are redrafted in Mu-jin's and Malphas's voices. The Papers keep their dry field-note prose with names and mechanics fixed, and the new investigator's card is built from that voice. About 4,300 fewer words redrafted.

questions.rec_reason: Rewrite where the narrator's life actually changes and keep proven prose where it does not. The Papers' author has no card yet, so the Papers become that card's source rather than a voice forced onto it.
questions.evidence: Word files: Vol I 4,779, Vol II 5,296, Vol III 6,603, Necrocursica 6,394, Papers 4,297 words; Alftian Codex meta page 41-43; Mu-jin's card 25-32; Malphas's card 20

sections.title: The texts' own story, cast and names
sections.intro: What happens inside the three texts' shared plot, and to each supporting character, before the authors change. The cast items come early because the Mu-jin and Malphas questions lean on them.

questions.title: Real historical names in the texts
questions.question: Which Earth names stay: those of real historical people, those of gods and literary figures, and the Emerald Tablet's wording?
questions.context: The texts borrow real people: Paracelsus (Swiss physician; the name means 'beyond Celsus', and no Celsus exists in the world), Jabir ibn Hayyan (eighth-century alchemist), and echoes in Gillus De Raits (Gilles de Rais, executed for murdering children) and Vaughaus Thom (Thomas Vaughan). They borrow Hermetic figures: Trismegistus (an epithet of the god Hermes), Asclepius (a god), Tat (a pupil in the dialogues), and three English Emerald Tablet translations. Rules allow god, demon and saint names on beings (R50-05) and idea-names anywhere (R48-22).

options.label: Keep them all
options.consequence: Fastest; R50-05 is extended to historical persons by ruling. Readers who know Gilles de Rais will read Gillus as a child-killer, which the texts never pay off.

options.label: Rename historical people; keep gods and idea-names
options.consequence: Furveus loses 'Paracelsus'; Jabir, Gillus and Thom get in-world names; Trismegistus and Asclepius stay under R50-05; Tat is renamed unless he becomes Doyun; the Tablet's wording and the Tria Prima stay, credited in author notes (R48-27).

options.label: Rename every Earth-derived personal name
options.consequence: B plus new names for Tat and Asclepius, and 'Trismegistus' leaves canon; only idea-names and the Tablet's wording stay.

options.label: Keep only names the texts explain in-world
options.consequence: Trismegistus stays (glossed in-world as 'three parts of the wisdom'); Paracelsus and Jabir go; the others are judged one by one.

questions.rec_reason: It applies R50-05 and R48-22 as written, needs no new rule, and removes the one echo that carries a real atrocity. Whether Mu-jin claims 'Trismegistus' is a separate question.
questions.evidence: rules R50-05, R48-22, R48-27, R51-06; overview 41-47; wiki Volume the First 22, 93, 145; Volume III 402

questions.title: When Thom's fourth-residue paper was written
questions.question: Thom's sealed paper is twelve years old, yet Volume III says he took the method from a commission about two years ago: which reading holds?
questions.context: The Papers and Volume III keep Thom's paper sealed at Genesio for twelve years, and Thom says he spent twelve years activating old traces (waking dead people's leftover records). Volume III says he took the framework from Madeleine Ault's commission, yet calls his paper independent. The Papers' line 75 dates the paper twelve years after the Necrocursica. The order decides who found the fourth residue (the Volitional Trace, a dead person's unfinished decision) first, and when the Tempus drift began.

options.label: Old paper on the residue; completion method after the commission
options.consequence: The twelve-year paper and crude activations stay; the completion method and the drift date from the commission, and Volume III line 122 reads as the completion step only. Papers line 75 is reworded, or it puts the Necrocursica's first edition about 24 years back.

options.label: Everything after the commission
options.consequence: Every 'twelve years' shrinks (Papers lines 75, 101; Volume III lines 150, 298) and Volume III line 280's 'independently' is reread. Madeleine's priority and the drift's start hold; the archivist's shelving beat shrinks to under two years.

options.label: Everything before the commission, method included
options.consequence: Thom had the residue and the completion method twelve years ago; Gillus's line 122 claim becomes vanity. Line 340's order changes, and twelve years of full activation must explain why the drift began only eighteen months ago (Papers line 205).

questions.rec_reason: Volume III already treats the paper as early, independent work (lines 150, 280, 298, 340), it keeps the shelved paper the Heresiology's non-commitment corruption describes, and the drift still starts with the commission.
questions.evidence: Corrant Papers 75, 93, 101, 205; Volume III 122, 150, 188, 280, 298, 340; Heresiology, Separation Perverted ('shelves it without alert')

questions.title: Credit for the Volitional Trace and commission
questions.question: Who first found the Volitional Trace, who named it, who built the method, and who designed the grief commission?
questions.context: The Volitional Trace is the record of a decision someone died while making. Volume II has the narrator write 'I call it the Volitional Trace'; Gillus's letter to the investigator says 'The Volitional Trace theory is my work'; Volume III credits Madeleine first, Thom independently and Gillus with the name; the Necrocursica credits De Raits, Thom and the narrator. Volume III says Gillus designed the method and Madeleine the commission. The overview page states one chain as fact.

options.label: Layered credit, and Mu-jin names it
options.consequence: Madeleine found it and designed the commission; Thom found it independently; Gillus framed the theory and built the mechanism; Mu-jin coined the name. Edit Volume III lines 66, 340 and overview line 63; Necrocursica line 93 credits Mu-jin as namer, not co-builder.

options.label: Volume III's chain as written; Gillus names it
options.consequence: Volume II's 'I call it' becomes Mu-jin adopting Gillus's term, and Necrocursica line 93 drops him. Mu-jin stays the outside witness; only Volume II line 261, the overview and line 93 change.

options.label: Gillus owns it
options.consequence: His letter is true and Volume III's chain is Mu-jin's generosity. Volume II's 'I call it' goes, Madeleine shrinks to a supporting role, and Mu-jin gains nothing from the discovery.

options.label: Leave the disagreement as unreliable narration
options.consequence: No edits to the five texts (the Lore & History hub calls the Codex 'unreliable by construction'), but the overview page and Necrocursica line 93 stop stating one chain as settled fact.

questions.rec_reason: Three edits make each text true at its own level; naming fits his matured Anamnesis (the memory Wellspring), which 'reads inherited intention', and naming is not building, so his Arena condemnation of the method stays honest.
questions.evidence: Volume II 261; Corrant Papers 255; Volume III 66, 274, 340; Necrocursica 93; overview 63; Mu-jin's card, Harmonizations; Arena interjection scene 25

questions.title: One letter from Gillus or two
questions.question: Is there one letter from Gillus to the narrator or two, and which one sat unopened for four months?
questions.context: Volume II transcribes a Gillus letter: 'received... not answered'. The Papers' case file holds 'one unanswered letter', an original, 'which suggests someone intercepted it'. Volume III has the investigator deliver a letter the narrator 'did not open for four months', and Halveth notes 'He answered the letter'. One letter cannot be transcribed, intercepted and delivered unopened at once. The Necrocursica's own 'four months' concerns his copy of that treatise and matches Volume II's 'resisted reading it for some months'.

options.label: Two letters
options.consequence: Volume II's letter was received and transcribed; a second was intercepted, held in the case file, hand-delivered by the investigator, unopened four months, then answered. Papers line 23 and Volume III line 78 say 'second'; the Necrocursica's note stays as an echo.

options.label: One letter, intercepted
options.consequence: Volume II cannot have transcribed it, so its chapter 8 becomes a later insertion that Mu-jin must explain inside the text.

options.label: One letter, never intercepted
options.consequence: The Papers' 'original... intercepted' and Volume III's delivery are cut; the investigator's doorway beat in Volume III's prologue goes, and so does Mu-jin's thank-you letter for it.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps every scene, including the doorway delivery and Mu-jin's thank-you letter, and needs two phrase edits.
questions.evidence: Volume II 89, 183-201; Corrant Papers 23, 225; Volume III 18, 76-80, 350; Necrocursica 25

questions.title: Eleven days or fourteen
questions.question: How long did the reconstructed likeness of Madeleine Ault last before it ended: eleven days or fourteen?
questions.context: The impression-body (a likeness rebuilt from a dead person's traces) is timed three ways in the Papers: 'It lasted eleven days' (line 133), 'On the eleventh day, it began to change' (135), and 'On the fourteenth day' it asks for her workroom (139). Volume III line 276 says Madeleine planned 'eleven days of sufficient coherence to locate and direct him'. Canon is silent on how long such a body lasts, so this becomes its first stated limit.

options.label: Eleven days in all
options.consequence: Line 139 becomes 'Before the eleventh day was out'. Lines 133 and 135 and Volume III line 276 stay true; the change, the request and the ending fall on the last day.

options.label: Eleven coherent days, fourteen in all
options.consequence: Line 133 becomes 'It held for eleven days'; line 139 stays; Volume III line 276 gains a clause that for three more days her decision, not her likeness, did the directing. This adds a rule: a Trace outlasts its likeness.

questions.rec_reason: One phrase edit makes all four lines agree and gives the impression-body one clean stated limit, eleven days, which Madeleine designed around.
questions.evidence: Corrant Papers 133, 135, 139, 185; Volume III 276; The Crossing 52-54 (silent on impression-bodies)

questions.title: What happens to Paracelsus (Furveus)
questions.question: Does Furveus, called Paracelsus, stay a new person, become an existing character, or fold into Gillus?
questions.context: Furveus is the iatrochemist (a physician who treats with prepared metals and salts) who takes the grief commission, builds the likeness and afterwards checks his hands. The Necrocursica calls him its author's colleague from the Heralds' Medical University, credits him with its stabilisation protocol and gives him 'Tell them not to be afraid of the dead'. 'Paracelsus' borrows a real Swiss physician. No card holds the commission or a friendship with Mu-jin; Cael Dareth, a mercury-scarred alchemist expelled from the Accord's Research and Archives Division, is nearest.

options.label: Keep as a new person named Furveus
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short minor-NPC record) with a FOW (Fracture of Worlds, the stat system) line pricing the commission; 'called Paracelsus' follows ST1. Through the Necrocursica he is Malphas's colleague too, a tie Malphas's card must carry.

options.label: He is Cael Dareth, the Pale Crucible
options.consequence: Cael's card gains the Medical University, the commission and a friendship with Mu-jin. The genial Furveus takes Cael's voice ('an equation solved aloud'), and Cael's written Lore (Varūn, a Division bench at Stannvaard, expulsion) must make room for Castlefall.

options.label: Fold him into Gillus
options.consequence: Gillus executes his own commission. The lower-room laboratory, the coffee scene and 'The footnote is correct' become a confrontation with Gillus, and the Codex loses the friend who crosses the line.

questions.rec_reason: He is the Codex's human cost, and Cael's written Lore and voice hold no genial friend at Castlefall; a roster entry prices the working without forcing a card.
questions.evidence: Volume I ch. 2; Volume II 23-63, 125, 271; Necrocursica 121, 169, 397, 455; Cael Dareth's card 24-29, Lore

questions.title: What happens to Gillus De Raits
questions.question: Does Gillus De Raits become a new person with a full card, a lighter roster entry, or an existing character?
questions.context: Gillus runs through four texts: he compels the Necrocursica's author, arranges the commission, writes the letters and meets the narrator on the Castlefall railway platform. Volume III reads him as Stage VII (a rank of soul growth) with Mortalis (the death Wellspring) primary and Anamnesis (memory) secondary. His name echoes Gilles de Rais, a fifteenth-century French lord executed for murdering children. Moros Pellayne, the Arbitration Division's necro-jurist, holds 'the trace is not the soul' but is Anamnesis-primary and Stage VIII.

options.label: New person with a full character card
options.consequence: A full card with a FOW (Fracture of Worlds) loadout, costs, counters and a Voice block; name per ST1. Mu-jin's and Malphas's cards both gain him in Ties.

options.label: New person, roster entry only
options.consequence: A roster record (want, refusal, lie, voice) and a one-line stat summary; lighter and upgradeable, but his Stage VII working stays unpriced meanwhile.

options.label: He is Moros Pellayne, the Ossuary Registrar
options.consequence: An Arbitration Division forensic officer becomes Malphas's compeller and the commission's designer. Moros's card gains the six-year correspondence and the platform meeting, his Wellspring order flips to Mortalis first, and Volume III's Stage VII becomes VIII.

questions.rec_reason: He is the shared antagonist of four texts and the man who compels Malphas, so fair play needs his loadout, costs and a findable counter on the page.
questions.evidence: Volume III 46-66; Corrant Papers 241-275; Necrocursica 37-45; Moros Pellayne's card 15, 44, 128

questions.title: What happens to Vaughaus Thom
questions.question: Does Vaughaus Thom, who scaled the completion method at Genesio, stay a new person, fold into Malphas, or fold into Gillus?
questions.context: Thom is in his late sixties, restless and curious; he activated old traces at Genesio to finish dead people's work, left the oldest Trace alone and agrees to stop. His work is the Heresiology's (canon's book of alchemical corruption) Case IV, whose lesson is that Fermentation Perverted (prizing rot because it yields results) 'arrives crowned with achievements', the tell Malphas's card carries. His name echoes Thomas Vaughan, a seventeenth-century Welsh alchemist.

options.label: Keep as a new person
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short NPC record) with a FOW stat line (Anamnesis, crude impression-bodies, twelve years' activation); name per ST1. Malphas stays the theorist whose architecture Thom scaled, so his card's tell becomes a line he lives into later.

options.label: Fold his activation project into Malphas
options.consequence: Malphas runs Genesio and sits at Volume III's fire with Mu-jin, settling the Night Watch bible's open question of whether Mu-jin knows Salter (Malphas's teaching alias); the Necrocursica's 'what Vaughaus Thom replicated' becomes self-reference.

options.label: Fold him into Gillus
options.consequence: Gillus scales his own method. Thom's 'not what I intended' line, Volume III's three-man fire scene and the old man's floor go, and Case IV's operator becomes the letter-writer.

questions.rec_reason: Thom's curiosity with a floor is the Codex's counterweight to Gillus, and keeping him lets Malphas's canon tell land later instead of being spent here.
questions.evidence: Volume III 120-150, 180, 298-308; Heresiology Case IV; Malphas's card 45-47; Night Watch bible 153; Necrocursica 173

questions.title: What happens to Neros
questions.question: Does Neros, the quiet astronomer who catches the Tempus drift, stay a new person, fold into the Accord's observation post, or become an existing character?
questions.context: Neros is the third friend, quiet, a collector of star charts. He rides to Urbis with the narrator; his instruments catch the drift of Tempus (the gas giant in the sky), his readings sit in the Papers' case file and the Accord's post at Naln verifies them. The Heresiology's (canon's corruption casebook) Case V retells the drift without naming anyone. The nearest card, Orivane Caelthys, is a Stage X navigator of the Concord Celestial Cartography Office, not a quiet friend.

options.label: Keep as a new person
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short NPC record) and a voice note; the railway conversation, the stabilised drift and the case-file readings stay. Where he met Mu-jin follows the origin question.

options.label: Fold him into the observation post at Naln
options.consequence: Accord instruments, not a friend, catch the drift. Volume II's railway conversation becomes Mu-jin reading a report, and Volume I's company shrinks by one.

options.label: He is Orivane Caelthys, the Astral Shepherd
options.consequence: A Stage X navigator becomes a chart-collecting companion; his card gains the Codex years and a friendship with Mu-jin, and his quiet must be written against his public office.

questions.rec_reason: His part is small and human, the case file needs his readings, and Orivane's public Stage X office would swamp a quiet railway friendship.
questions.evidence: Volume I ch. 1; Volume II 211-229, 263; Corrant Papers 23-25; Heresiology Case V; Orivane Caelthys's card 30

questions.title: What happens to Jabir
questions.question: Does Jabir, the roadside astrologer who gives the amulet and the correspondence doctrine, stay a new person, become Geuk-hon, or fold into the dragon-claw monk?
questions.context: Emerald-eyed Jabir, from 'eastern lands', teaches 'as above, so below' at an attic telescope, recites the Emerald Tablet (an old Hermetic text) and gives the copper amulet and the copper pen. Volume III calls him 'Jabir ibn Hayyan', a real eighth-century alchemist. The mapping audit offered Geuk-hon, Mu-jin's counsel who speaks like 'a man describing something he had already watched happen once', but Geuk-hon comes after the orchard at 24 and may be his prior soul.

options.label: Keep as a new person
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short NPC record); his name, and Volume III's 'ibn Hayyan', follow ST1. His homeland follows the setting question on the Shaneni empire, a polity canon lacks.

options.label: He is Geuk-hon
options.consequence: The Jabir meeting moves to Mu-jin's 24th year or later, and Geuk-hon gains a body, a telescope and an eastern origin; this collides with any ruling that makes the old Trace Geuk-hon's earlier life.

options.label: Fold him into the dragon-claw monk
options.consequence: One Monastery teacher recites the Tablet and gives the amulet and the grief lesson. Volume I loses one of three Tablet recitations, and the pen and Volume III's 'Jabir's doctrine' credit move to the monk.

questions.rec_reason: His amulet, pen and doctrine run through all three volumes, and Geuk-hon's canon (after the orchard, possibly a prior soul) cannot hold a middle-aged man in an attic.
questions.evidence: Volume I ch. 3; Volume II 75, 221; Volume III 402; 03_wren_three_deliveries 179-183, 228; Mu-jin's card Lore

questions.title: What happens to Tat
questions.question: Does Tat, the student who wept for his cat and asked the Third Corruption question, stay a new person, become Doyun, or go?
questions.context: Tat is the narrator's assigned Monastery partner: he loses his cat, hears 'None of the things that are, are truly destroyed', and in Volume II asks what the Corruption of Separation is (the Third Corruption: seeing clearly and not acting), then is given the Necrocursica author's address. Doyun, the one left of the nine students in Mu-jin's room at Sum-gol, is earnest and applies lessons 'taught by you personally'; he is 15 when Mu-jin is 24. 'Tat' is Hermes's pupil in the Hermetic dialogues.

options.label: Keep as a new person
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short NPC record); name per ST1. The Monastery scenes stay as they are and no canon student changes.

options.label: He is Doyun, met as a boy
options.consequence: Tat's scenes move from the Monastery to Mu-jin's room at Sum-gol, when Doyun is about 13 to 15 (Mu-jin 22 to 24). Doyun gains the cat, the Third Corruption question and the address; his boyhood becomes canon.

options.label: Cut him
options.consequence: The cat lesson and the Third Corruption's prompt go to Asclepius or to Mu-jin's own reflection, and Volume II's appendix loses its student.

questions.rec_reason: Doyun's archived voice (a lesson 'taught by you personally', slate held to his chest) is Tat's earnest one, and it gives the one student left of nine a history with his teacher.
questions.evidence: Volume I ch. 3; Volume II 231, 267; WOTR_Vaeloris_Sequence 41, 1904-1934; Mu-jin's card Lore (nine students, Doyun left)

questions.title: What happens to Madeleine Ault
questions.question: How does Madeleine Ault, the dying scholar who designed her own commission, enter canon?
questions.context: Madeleine is dead before the texts open. A scholar in Anamnesis-adjacent practice (Anamnesis: the Wellspring of memory), she found the fourth residue, cleared her workroom, sealed a document and, per Volume III, designed the commission so her likeness would lead her husband to it. The Heresiology (canon's corruption casebook) holds her unnamed as Case III, 'The Eastern Commission of Grief'. Fair play needs her Trace priced: her Stage (rank of soul growth) and attunement decide how strong it was.

options.label: New person with a roster entry and stat line
options.consequence: A short NPC record (dead of lung-sickness; Anamnesis-adjacent scholar; her Stage) with a FOW (Fracture of Worlds) stat line that prices her Trace and the eleven days. Case III stays unnamed.

options.label: Named in the texts only, no record
options.consequence: Nothing new in the roster; the strength of her Trace stays unstated, so the eleven days have no cost behind them.

options.label: Fold her discovery into Gillus
options.consequence: She becomes only the dead wife; Volume III's 'She designed the commission' and chapter four's account of her go, and the Trace becomes Gillus's alone.

questions.rec_reason: She is the Codex's best-designed working and the Trace needs a cost; a roster entry with a stat line prices it without a full card for someone never seen alive.
questions.evidence: Volume II 27; Volume III 272-284; Corrant Papers 143-147; Heresiology Case III

questions.title: What happens to Cassian Ault
questions.question: Does Cassian Ault, the widower who paid for the commission, become a roster NPC, stay a name in the texts, or become a nameless role?
questions.context: Cassian is a wealthy man of about sixty in the eastern lowlands. He waited two years, paid through Gillus, received the likeness, opened his late wife's workroom at its request and will not tell the investigator what her sealed document said. He is the mourner of the Heresiology's Case III (canon's grief-commission case). The naming rule R50-27 says a new person who speaks twice or matters gets a name. No card holds a widower of this kind.

options.label: Roster NPC through the NPC build
options.consequence: A record with a want, a refusal line, a lie (what the document said) and a voice, so the Papers' interview has a person behind it and a later scene can use him.

options.label: Named in the texts only
options.consequence: No roster record; his interview stands as written and any later scene needs a build first.

options.label: Reduce him to 'the nobleman'
options.consequence: Volume II already calls him that; the Papers drop his name, which breaks R50-27 because he gives an account and matters to the case.

questions.rec_reason: He holds a secret the investigator cannot open, which is exactly what a refusal line and a lie are for, and it costs one record.
questions.evidence: Volume II 27, 57; Corrant Papers 113-155; Heresiology Case III; naming rule R50-27

questions.title: What happens to Halveth
questions.question: Is Halveth the quiet power behind the Research and Archives Division's Urbis office, behind the whole Division, or folded into Dessa Mael?
questions.context: Halveth assigns the investigator the case, speaks through margin notes and, per Volume III, has been 'the Research Division's effective director for eleven years while appearing to be an annotator'; Gillus clears 'no sanctions' with her. Canon's Research and Archives Division (the Accord's scholarship and archive branch) has an unnamed head, appointed and dismissed by the High Concordant, and its rivals fear it 'Nobody openly. Everybody quietly'. No card fits her.

options.label: New person, quiet director of the Urbis office
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short NPC record); the twist stays regional, and 'the Research Division' in the Papers and Volume III means its Urbis branch. No Division head changes.

options.label: New person, quiet power behind the whole Division
options.consequence: She fills canon's unnamed head by influence, not office; the Guild Accord's Modern Era page gains her, and every Division plot must allow a woman in Urbis steering it.

options.label: Fold her into Dessa Mael
options.consequence: One archivist both keeps the Genesio stacks and runs the case, and she becomes the one who let Thom's paper sit, the Heresiology's example of non-commitment.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps her twist and the no-sanctions ruling at the scale the texts need, without seating a hidden power over a Division whose head the High Concordant appoints.
questions.evidence: Corrant Papers 17, 29, 203, 219-225; Volume III 310-324; Guild Accord Modern Era page 53, 62

questions.title: What happens to the king
questions.question: Does the unquestioned king of Volume I stay an unnamed ruler, become the Mahuo court's monarch, or go?
questions.context: An elected ruler of a city-state near Urbis beats his wife and dismisses every adviser; the Monastery sends the narrator, whose recitation makes him weep and govern gently. Canon already holds him as the Heresiology's (canon's corruption casebook) Case I, 'The Hall of the Unquestioned King', the example of Calcination Perverted (certainty that no longer hears contradiction). He never speaks a quoted line. Mu-jin's card has a royal court that made him the Ledger-Prince but says nothing of its king.

options.label: Unnamed ruler, a role
options.consequence: No card; he and his wife stay roles, as R50-27 allows for a man with no lines. Case I and Volume II's use of him stay.

options.label: He is the monarch of the Mahuo court
options.consequence: The rebuke becomes personal, but the text's 'elected... city-state in the Urbis orbit' goes, and wife-beating enters Mu-jin's own royal house, which canon has never described.

options.label: Cut the chapter
options.consequence: Case I loses its source scene, Volume II's Calcination Perverted example needs another, and the third Tablet recitation goes.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already holds him as Case I without a name, and naming him adds a person the texts never needed.
questions.evidence: Volume I ch. 4; wiki Volume the First 130-146; Heresiology Case I; Mu-jin's card 30

questions.title: What happens to Asclepius
questions.question: Does Asclepius, the High Elf teacher who listened without converting, stay a new person, become an existing character, or fold into Frithia?
questions.context: Asclepius is the Monastery's primary teacher, a High Elf and an atheist who finds God-Essence (the texts' divine current) an embarrassing relic; the narrator teaches her, and she 'did not convert. She listened'. Her name belongs to a Greek god, which the naming rule R50-05 allows on a being. The nearest card, Serenyra Vaelith, is a High Elf called 'High Archivist of Resonance'. Frithia, Mu-jin's wife, doubted written-down knowledge until she watched him face a Legion-class working at 22.

options.label: Keep as a new person
options.consequence: A roster entry (a short NPC record); her name follows ST1. Her atheism follows the setting ruling on God-Essence.

options.label: She is Serenyra Vaelith
options.consequence: An immensely powerful neutral Archmagus becomes a monastery teacher whom Mu-jin instructs, and her card, whose gloss rights keep her interior closed, gains the Codex years.

options.label: Fold her into Frithia
options.consequence: The memoir gains his wife, but Frithia is from the ice country, not an elf, and changed her mind by witness, not argument; the scene must move to the Legion-class working at 22.

questions.rec_reason: Her part is one teaching exchange, and neither Serenyra's standing nor Frithia's archived change of mind fits it without bending their cards.
questions.evidence: wiki Volume the First 122; Serenyra Vaelith's card, Identity; wotr_the_warrior_nurse 31, 67; naming rule R50-05

questions.title: What happens to Dessa Mael
questions.question: Does Dessa Mael, the Genesio lower-stacks archivist, stay a new person, fold into Halveth, or become an existing archivist?
questions.context: Dessa Mael has kept the sealed stacks of the Genesio Archivum (where the Necrocursica is held) longer than the investigator has been alive; she finds the Thom submission, reads its review note and brings tea when someone needs a moment. Her 'carefully neutral' sentence names the institution's failure. The nearest card, Elowen Mireille, the Porcelain Archivist, also works through tea, but she is a young observer placed in noble households by the Ivory Ledger Society (a network of house-watchers).

options.label: Keep as a new person
options.consequence: A short NPC record (want, refusal, voice); the Genesio archive scene stays as written.

options.label: Fold her into Halveth
options.consequence: Halveth pulls the file herself; the Genesio scene loses its second voice and Halveth becomes the one who let the paper sit.

options.label: She is Elowen Mireille
options.consequence: Elowen leaves her household placements for a Genesio post and ages into an old keeper; her tea-table method gains an archive, and her Society ties need a reason to reach the sealed stacks.

questions.rec_reason: She is a small, well-drawn witness to the shelving, and no archivist card fits her age or post.
questions.evidence: Corrant Papers 71-105; Elowen Mireille's card, Identity and Lore 129-143

questions.title: What happens to the plagiarising lecturer
questions.question: Does the senior lecturer who faked plagiarism evidence stay an unnamed role, become Doryun, Mu-jin's estranged court mentor, or go?
questions.context: At the Herald's Medical University a narcissistic senior lecturer copies the students' own work back at them as plagiarism evidence, lunges at Paracelsus and takes a strike to the sternum; both degrees are revoked and Paracelsus wins them back. Mu-jin's card has Senior Alchemist Doryun, his court mentor, 'estranged... heavy, unresolved', whose foil line is 'patience without honesty'; the court credited the fourteen-year-old's correction rather than stealing it.

options.label: Unnamed role, scene as written
options.consequence: No card changes; the lecturer stays a role, as R50-27 allows. Where the University sits in Mu-jin's life follows the origin question.

options.label: He is Doryun, recut as quiet theft
options.consequence: The scene moves to the court: Doryun patiently signs his pupil's later work as his own, with no brawl, and Paracelsus's sternum strike goes. Doryun's card gains the act behind 'estranged', kept separate from the credited correction at fourteen.

options.label: Cut the scene
options.consequence: Volume I loses the revoked and retrieved degrees and Paracelsus's genial persuasion; his introduction rests on Spagyria (his three-part medicine) alone.

questions.rec_reason: The card's foil line, 'patience without honesty', describes this act, and it gives 'estranged, heavy, unresolved' an on-page cause; the brawl goes because Doryun's card is patience.
questions.evidence: wiki Volume the First 62-64; Mu-jin's card 30, 105, 121, 170, 191; Open Crucible 119

questions.title: What happens to the Prior and dragon-claw monk
questions.question: Do the Prior and the monk with the dragon-claw amulet stay unnamed roles, gain a name, merge, or map onto Doryun?
questions.context: The Prior welcomes the narrator ('everything'), writes to him of his manuscript and presides as the Sacred Discourse (the Monastery's assembly) raises him to the top tier. The dragon-claw monk, whose Dragon Hunter father died 'on Tempus-bred quarry', gives the grief lesson the narrator calls his 'most load-bearing entry'. Mu-jin's card says his court 'made him a symbol instead of a person' while his mentor Doryun stayed patient.

options.label: Both stay unnamed roles
options.consequence: No new records; the Monastery keeps two roles, and the monk's lesson stands without a person behind it.

options.label: Name the dragon-claw monk; the Prior stays a role
options.consequence: The monk gets a name and a short NPC record (want, voice, his father's death); the Prior stays a role. The father's death 'on Tempus-bred quarry' follows the setting ruling on Tempus.

options.label: Merge them into one Monastery elder
options.consequence: One elder welcomes him, gives the grief lesson and presides at the Sacred Discourse; Volume I loses a scene's worth of cast.

options.label: The Prior is Doryun
options.consequence: Works only if the Monastery becomes Mu-jin's court: the Sacred Discourse becomes the court making him the Ledger-Prince. It cannot combine with Doryun as the lecturer (ST18).

questions.rec_reason: The monk's lesson is the one the narrator calls load-bearing, which is what R50-27 means by 'matters'; the Prior acts mostly through reported speech and stays a role.
questions.evidence: Volume I vault docx 52-55, 66; wiki Volume the First 101-103, 123; Mu-jin's card 30, 105, 170; naming rule R50-27

questions.title: Are the three friends canon's three dead?
questions.question: Are Furveus, Neros and the friend who brings the Necrocursica the 'three of them are dead' Mu-jin thinks of at 24?
questions.context: At 24, with Ara changing his dressings, Mu-jin thinks there are perhaps four people alive who would have done what she did, 'and three of them are dead'. Canon never names the three. The Codex's three friends arrive together in Volume I; at the end of Volume II Paracelsus 'continues to work', and Volume III, set about six years after the commission, names him as a colleague.

options.label: Yes, the three Codex friends
options.consequence: Their deaths fall before Mu-jin is 24, so the Codex's events must end by then (K1), a closing note records each death, and Mu-jin's card gains three names in Ties.

options.label: Leave the line unassigned
options.consequence: No change; the friends' later fates stay open and the three dead can be anyone a later scene needs.

options.label: Paracelsus and Neros only
options.consequence: Two of the three are the Codex's and die before Mu-jin is 24; the third stays open, which leaves the Necrocursica friend's fate to the Malphas questions.

questions.rec_reason: Paracelsus is still working after the commission, and pinning three deaths before 24 would squeeze the whole Codex into the years before Vaeloris.
questions.evidence: WOTR_Vaeloris_Sequence 1808; wiki Volume the First 22; Volume II 271; Volume III 66, 402

questions.title: Correcting Nospheric, Anamnetic and Necrocursica
questions.question: Which of the texts' coined Greek and Latin words are corrected to real forms, and which stay as published?
questions.context: The naming law wants borrowed words correct in their source language (R50-01) but corrects a published name only 'where the name keeps its sound' (R50-02). 'Nospheric' reads as a misspelling of 'noospheric' (from Greek nous, mind), and canon already uses it once on the Sub-Stats page. 'Anamnetic' is attested in liturgical English beside the standard 'anamnestic'. 'Necrocursica' joins Greek necro- to a non-Latin ending. 'Urbis' is Latin for 'of the city', used as a name.

options.label: Fix only the plain misspelling
options.consequence: 'Nospheric' becomes 'Noospheric' in the Necrocursica (13 uses) and on the Sub-Stats page; Anamnetic, Necrocursica and Urbis stay as published.

options.label: Fix both adjectives
options.consequence: A, plus 'Anamnetic' becomes 'Anamnestic' across Volume III and the Necrocursica; Necrocursica and Urbis stay.

options.label: Leave all four
options.consequence: Nospheric is read as a coined in-world word, not a misspelling; no canon page changes.

options.label: Also retitle the Necrocursica
options.consequence: B, plus a correct Greek or Latin title for the treatise; the Heresiology's and overview's references change, and so does the sound, which R50-02 does not ask for.

questions.rec_reason: 'Nospheric' is a word nowhere and the fix barely moves its sound; the other three are attested or published names R50-02 leaves alone.
questions.evidence: rules R50-01, R50-02, R50-12; Necrocursica 105, 137; Sub-Stats page (Part Twelve) 91; Volume III (14 uses of Anamnetic)

questions.title: A Sum-gol title for Mu-jin's book
questions.question: Should Mu-jin's book carry a title in his house tongue beside 'The Alftian Codex', replace it, or have none?
questions.context: The naming law gives an item a name in each culture's tongue, listed side by side (R50-13), and Mahuo names come from the Korean stratum (R23-2, the Korean-based naming layer). Mu-jin's card says that in grief Concord Common leaves him and the house tongue of Sum-gol comes back. 'The Alftian Codex' reads as the archivists' shelf title, taken from the region where the events happened.

options.label: Add a Sum-gol title beside The Alftian Codex
options.consequence: A correct Korean-stratum title, his own name for the book, heads Volume I and the overview's name list; 'The Alftian Codex' stays the archive title everywhere else.

options.label: Make the Sum-gol title primary
options.consequence: Page titles, INDEX entries, the Heresiology's and Errata's references and the renames registry all change to the new title.

options.label: No Mahuo title
options.consequence: He wrote in Concord Common for an Accord archive; one name, no changes.

questions.rec_reason: R50-13 asks for side-by-side names, it puts his own voice on the cover, and it leaves every existing reference to the Codex intact.
questions.evidence: rules R50-13 ITEM_NAMES, R23-2 KOREAN_STRATUM; Mu-jin's card 141 (In grief); Errata to the Received Registers 39

sections.title: Kwon Mu-jin and the Codex
sections.intro: The Codex becomes Mu-jin's own memoir. These questions fit a terrace-farmer's Elfin narrator to a Mahuo court prodigy who is 38 today.

questions.title: When Sum-gol emptied, against Mu-jin's boyhood
questions.question: Which account of Sum-gol's end holds, so that Chapter the First knows what kind of valley Mu-jin grew up in?
questions.context: Sum-gol ('Breath Hollow') is the Mahuo home province in Ketsuen, and canon ends it three ways. The Primate's card: he was nine when it 'finished emptying', forty-nine years ago, long before Mu-jin's birth. The Vaeloris sequence: Ara 'was nine when Sum-gol went', about twelve years before Mu-jin's 24. The Ketsuen page: a living, self-governing province of about 15,000 with a Warden and Council seat. Mu-jin keeps a school there, and Kaalabad's strike falls on 'sixty roofs'. The character-lore pass let the Primate's card govern; no ruling or conflict row exists.

options.label: Before his birth: the Primate's card governs
options.consequence: He is born to the remnant of a house whose valley had already thinned; the school and the sixty roofs are what remained. Ara's 'Sum-gol went' reads as the last of the house going, as her scene already hints. No scene line changes.

options.label: In his boyhood, about twelve: Ara's line governs
options.consequence: Chapter the First ends with the valley emptying two years before his Catalyst (the corrected array at fourteen that made his name). The Primate's card breaks: his Catalyst, fracture log and 'forty-nine years open' are rewritten for a man who was forty-six then.

options.label: Never emptied as a place: the Ketsuen page governs
options.consequence: 'Finished emptying' narrows to the Primate's own hollow-seat kin and Ara's line to her branch of the house. Chapter the First becomes a court boyhood in a living province; the Primate's 'death of his entire people' is recut.

questions.rec_reason: The Primate's card hangs its Catalyst, fracture log and spirit axes on those forty-nine years, the lore pass already let it govern, and a thinned valley still fits the school, the sixty roofs and the Ketsuen page's province.
questions.evidence: Primate card (Catalyst, Spirit Axes, Fracture Log); Vaeloris:1900, :1976; Ketsuen:20, :68; Mu-jin card:162, :176; Kaalabad card:147-148; imports/lore/WEAVE.md R9

questions.title: What Chapter the First becomes
questions.question: Mu-jin was a court prodigy trained under Doryun, not a farm boy 'never meant' for learning; what does the Codex's opening chapter become?
questions.context: Chapter the First ('The Terraces') makes the narrator a terrace-farmer's son of the Alftian lowlands, ambushed by learning when a friend sets a primer on his kitchen table. Mu-jin's card: born to the Mahuo court line; grew up eleven miles from a mountain, carrying men down and learning 'how cold takes a hand'; trained under Doryun, the court's Senior Alchemist, until fourteen; then the Catalyst (a corrected Fixation array) and the title-writ grading him S-tier. Canon's only Sum-gol terrace belongs to the school he ran as an adult.

options.label: A Mahuo boyhood near the mountain, the house named once
options.consequence: The frost and the mountain come from his card, the fields from Sum-gol's river-valley farming; the sky-watching is new. He names the house once and the Ledger-Prince title (the court epithet he resents) never. 'No men of learning' goes.

options.label: Open on the Catalyst and the title-writ at fourteen
options.consequence: Chapter the First becomes the corrected array, the court turning him into a symbol, and the day he left with the lens. Tightest fit to the card; the frost chapter and its humility are lost, and the Codex becomes a story of leaving court.

options.label: He writes as nobody and leaves the court out
options.consequence: He omits his birth because of the Ledger-Prince wound (being used as proof of something), so the humble posture survives without a false parentage. Readers who know him see the gap, and one line must hint that he chose it.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already gives him the frost, the mountain and the men carried down, so the imagery survives honestly, and naming the house once but no title fits 'he gives his name and nothing above it'.
questions.evidence: Volume the First ch. 1 (wiki:18-24; vol1_vault:8-12); Mu-jin card:28-32, :137, :152, :162-164; Ketsuen:68; Warrior Nurse scene:3, :11

questions.title: Whose Trace waits for him, and whose tomb
questions.question: Now the narrator is a human Mahuo, whose 260-year unfinished decision completes into him at Genesio, and whose name is on the Mausoleum coffin?
questions.context: A Volitional Trace (the record of a decision someone died in the middle of making) has waited 260 years at Genesio, 'Elfin in constitution', 'for someone with your exact Aetheric signature'. In Vol I a coffin there reads 'Vis, Alchemical Astronomer', the old narrator's name. Canon: Kaalabad (the chained god-knight) calls Mu-jin 'GEUK-HON'; he answers 'That is not my name'. Geuk-hon says nobody 'in four hundred years' has taken enough away from him; only an author note calls Geuk-hon his prior soul. His Anamnesis (the memory Wellspring) reads 'inherited intention'.

options.label: His own earlier life: 'Vis' was the soul called Geuk-hon
options.consequence: The coffin keeps 'Vis, Alchemical Astronomer' as an Elfin earlier life of the soul Kaalabad names; that soul's four hundred years hold more than one life. Pays off Kaalabad and the Soul Kingdom thread, and makes the author note canon.

options.label: A Mahuo ancestor aimed it at the house's signature
options.consequence: The coffin names a Mahuo astronomer and 'Elfin in constitution' becomes Mahuo. Uses his inherited-intention reading with no earlier life, loses the link to Kaalabad, and makes him an heir rather than a return.

options.label: Aimed at a question, not a man; 'Vis' a stranger
options.consequence: 'Vis' stays an unrelated Elfin astronomer, and 'your exact signature' becomes 'the shape of the question you have been asking', so anyone asking it could have finished it. No soul canon; the Codex's thesis becomes literal.

questions.rec_reason: Two scenes and Kaalabad's card already point to an old soul under a name he refuses, and canon allows a reincarnational echo. A keeps the planted coffin clue and gives the retired name a real owner.
questions.evidence: Vol III docx:160-168; vol1_vault:21; 03_wren:179-183, :228; 10_mujin:123-127; Kaalabad card:151; Open Crucible:20; FoW VIII:26

questions.title: Where Ara appears in the Codex
questions.question: Ara travelled his teaching circuit for years, yet no sister appears in any volume; where does she appear?
questions.context: Every volume meets trouble without her: he studies medicine alone during his friends' illness, and Vol III is written 'at the request of no one'. Canon: 'Ara travelled his circuit with him'; she is a healer whose Mortalis undertone (a trace of the death Wellspring in her Essence) treats 'an ending as a passage'; her voice is plain, direct and dry. After Rimward, where he lost an eye, he told her: 'When I have something worth saying I will say it to you first.'

options.label: Healer in the illness chapter and Vol III's addressee
options.consequence: She treats the friends' illness beside him, and her 'ending as a passage' seeds the Monastery's 'Death is not the opposite of life'. Vol III is written to her, keeping the Rimward promise and replacing 'at the request of no one'.

options.label: Vol III's addressee only
options.consequence: Vols I–II stay without her; Vol III opens as the thing worth saying, said to her first. Smallest change, but the road volumes read as a gap unless one line admits the omission.

options.label: Healer in Vols I–II only; Vol III unaddressed
options.consequence: She shares the illness chapter and the road; Vol III stays 'at the request of no one'. Keeps the ending's solitude but leaves the Rimward promise unkept on the page.

options.label: Absent, and he admits why
options.consequence: One passage owns that he left her out the Mahuo way, settling her place without asking her. It cuts against his canon letter refusing exactly that ('So I am asking you instead'), and her voice is lost.

questions.rec_reason: Both cards put her on his circuit, her Mortalis undertone is the Codex's own subject, and his Rimward promise gives Vol III its reader. A letter to her also carries his voice under R51-33.
questions.evidence: Mu-jin card:163, :176, :178; Ara card:24, :42, :104, :128, :177; Vaeloris:1876-1880; Volume the First:35; Vol III docx:5; R51-33

questions.title: Which corruption Mu-jin finds in himself
questions.question: Which of the seven corruptions does Mu-jin recognise in himself across the Codex, given his card says he never lets an error sit?
questions.context: A corruption is one stage of the seven-stage Great Work (alchemy's path of refinement) turned against itself. Vol II's narrator finds Separation Perverted (Non-Commitment: 'perfect diagnosis, absent intervention') in himself: the letter left unanswered, the fourth residue filed as 'Gillus's problem'. 'I had simply decided not to be responsible for it.' Mu-jin's Flaw: 'Cannot let an error sit uncorrected.' Yet at Vaeloris he says of neglecting himself: 'I have decided that is a fault… and I have not done anything about it.'

options.label: Conviction (Calcination Perverted): certainty sealed against contradiction
options.consequence: The letter goes unanswered because it challenges the Aphorism he wrote 'describing someone else', and the corruption he saw in the king proves his own. Vol II's order, Vol III's 'Third Corruption' lines, the Papers' postscript and the Necrocursica's Appendix II are recut.

options.label: Separation turned inward: he corrects everyone but himself
options.consequence: He confronts Paracelsus and Gillus plainly; what he files away is his own matter, the Trace aimed at his signature. Vol II's confession survives nearly word for word, the café walk-out goes, and Vol III becomes the Heresiology's cure, a decision under witness.

options.label: Sanitized Truth (Distillation Perverted): clean theory without burden
options.consequence: He turns the commission's horror into elegant diagrams, 'I am only recording facts', matching his Distillatio Seal, whose cost falls on the asker. Breaks Vol II's order, where Separation is named from his own life.

questions.rec_reason: His own Vaeloris sentence nearly quotes the Codex's confession, so canon already shows this corruption in him. It keeps Vol II's order and its unanswered-letter spine, and needs no exception to his Flaw.

questions.title: How much of the Codex's ironic voice survives
questions.question: How much of the Codex's ornate, ironic narration survives as Mu-jin's written voice?
questions.context: The Codex narrates in lacquered irony: 'Pride is an unreasonable organ'; 'the way Urbis-educated men layer names like lacquer'. Mu-jin's card: formally precise, over-explains, apologises for explaining 'less often than he used to', notices the flaw first and then the child in the path, laughs nervously then looks severe; it lists no wit or irony. R51-33 (live) wants in-world letters 'in the writer's voice'. The king's-hall line 'remarkable or insufferable depending on the listener's disposition' already sounds like him.

options.label: A written voice built on his habits, changing by volume
options.consequence: Vol I apologises for explaining; by Vol III he has stopped. He notices the flaw, then the child. Lacquered jokes are cut back to dry self-correction. Length and texture stay, the man is recognisable, and the change shows his growth.

options.label: His speaking register throughout
options.consequence: Medium, steady teaching sentences, nothing ornate. Most faithful to the card, but much of the Codex's texture and length goes, and the three volumes read alike.

options.label: Keep the irony as his private page-voice
options.consequence: His card gains one line: on paper he is drier and funnier than he ever lets himself be aloud. The prose survives almost intact; readers must accept a man who writes unlike he speaks.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the Codex's best asset while meeting the writer's-voice rule, and the shift across three volumes puts his Dialogue Evolution ('now he simply corrects them') on the page.
questions.evidence: Mu-jin card:122-124, :133-142; Volume the First:22, :35; vol1_vault:74; R51-33 (doc-vocabulary-law:839-849)

questions.title: What happens to 'Trismegistus' and the Sage titles
questions.question: What becomes of 'Trismegistus', 'Sage of the Anamnetic Line, Keeper of the Correspondence' and 'Alftian Savant', given Mu-jin never claims a title?
questions.context: The narrator's name Trismegistus ('thrice-great', for holding three parts of the world's wisdom) is claimed inside the Emerald Tablet (an ancient alchemical text) he recites to move a king; Vol III's title page calls him Sage and Keeper; letters call him 'the Savant'. R52-21 (live): he never uses rank or court honorifics to win an argument; his card: 'he gives his name and nothing above it'. He resents his court epithet, the Ledger-Prince. Whether real historical names stay at all is asked separately.

options.label: Frame only: the archivists' title pages, never his words
options.consequence: Sage, Keeper and Savant appear only on the archive's title pages and colophon, an irony he would have hated; his own text never uses them. The Codex page's 'a claim he makes once' goes.

options.label: An epithet others gave him, which he refuses
options.consequence: After the king's hall the Monastery calls him 'the Thrice-Great'; he writes 'That is not my name', the line he later gives Kaalabad. The word stays in-world and rhymes with the Ledger-Prince; the frame's Sage titles go.

options.label: Drop every title everywhere
options.consequence: Title pages read 'Kwon Mu-jin' and, where dated, his Accord rank as the archive files it. Cleanest against R52-21, but it loses a motif the Codex carries through three volumes.

questions.rec_reason: It turns a rule-breaking boast into the scar his card already carries, a room naming him before he names himself, answered in the words canon gave him on the Ashgate road.
questions.evidence: R52-21 (doc-voice-law:569); Mu-jin card:24, :137, :152; 10_mujin:127; Volume the First:145; Vol III docx:5; Codex page:13, :41; Vol II docx:183

questions.title: Why a living man's journals sit sealed
questions.question: Why are a living teacher's journals 'recovered from the sealed lower stacks', and what do the archive's frame lines become?
questions.context: Every volume is framed as a 'Recovered Journal', 'Transcribed by the Silent Archivists', 'Recovered from the sealed lower stacks of the Herald's Archivum, Urbis', 'Restricted Access'; Vol III is 'Final Testimonies', the colophon his 'life's work', its last line 'Filed and sealed'. Mu-jin is alive at 38. His Desire: alchemy and summoning as 'common inheritance instead of court or bloodline property'. The Heresiology's archive duty: 'Redaction is guided survivability.' The Papers' investigator reads the Codex in a case file.

options.label: He filed them openly; the Accord sealed them
options.consequence: He deposits each volume under his teaching vow for common use; the Accord classifies them Mortalis-adjacent. 'Recovered' becomes 'withdrawn under seal'. His open book made restricted doctrine without asking him is the Ledger-Prince wound again.

options.label: Private journals, seized as evidence in the Genesio case
options.consequence: The Accord took his journals when the investigator opened the file. 'Recovered' becomes 'held as evidence', and Vol III's 'for the benefit of anyone willing' goes, since he never meant them for readers.

options.label: He sealed them himself
options.consequence: Fearing what the Mortalis material enables, he files them under his own seal, as Vol III's last line says. A sharp self-restriction for a man who wants knowledge common; his card needs a line on why.

questions.rec_reason: It fits his Desire, the Restricted stamps, the investigator's case-file access and the Heresiology's archive duty, and gives the frame his card's own wound: a room deciding what his work is for.
questions.evidence: Codex page:13-15; Lore & History:15, :43; vol1_vault:2-3, :92; Vol III docx:5, :402-406; Mu-jin card:27, :119, :152; Heresiology:216-225

questions.title: Whose hand wrote the unsigned margin note
questions.question: Whose hand wrote Vol III's epigraph, the margin note 'in handwriting that is not' the author's, found in a personal copy of Vol II?
questions.context: The note: 'The Philosopher who reaches the end of the Great Work and finds himself reflected in it has not failed the Work. He has finally begun it.' Vol III says Gillus De Raits 'has been corresponding with you through your own text for six years without signing his name'. The Necrocursica holds the mirror image, a margin note by the Codex's author in its Archivum copy. Mu-jin's Arena speech names a 'controlled archive' and 'the same source material'. Ara's voice is plain, direct and dry.

options.label: Gillus De Raits, corresponding unsigned through the text
options.consequence: The epigraph becomes Gillus's side of the six-year correspondence Vol III already describes, with no new canon. Mu-jin reads the answer in his own book before he answers the letter, which sharpens the unanswered-letter arc.

options.label: Malphas, writing back in the book paired with his
options.consequence: Mirrors the Necrocursica's margin note and ties the two authors through an object players can examine. It depends on how the Malphas questions set their acquaintance, and the aphorism reads as irony from a future lich.

options.label: Ara, in the copy he gave her
options.consequence: Her hand answers the brother who promised her the first word. The aphorism must be recut into her plain, direct voice, and Vol II must reach her before Vol III is written.

questions.rec_reason: Vol III already says Gillus corresponded through the text for six years without signing; the unsigned hand is that correspondence made visible. It costs no new canon and leaves Malphas's tie to the Malphas questions.
questions.evidence: Vol III docx:10, :66, :78; Necrocursica:25; Arena scene:25, :51; Ara card:128; Vaeloris:1880

questions.title: His Accord standing inside the Codex
questions.question: How does the Codex show that the Accord graded and posted Mu-jin and later made him Archmagus, when the texts tie him only to Herald institutions?
