options.label: Crystal layers by plane: Sulphur Core, Salt Shell, Mercury Attraction
options.consequence: Spagyria becomes layer-by-layer medicine; Separate-Purify-Recombine runs the Parting, Distillation and the Wedding, so it carries Conjunction's Rupture risk. The Necrocursica's Aetheric Shell residue joins Salt; its residue triad stays Malphas's openly 'modified' reading.

options.label: Crystal layers by behaviour: Core burns, Shell moves, Attraction binds
options.consequence: Sulphur Core, Mercury Shell, Salt Attraction Layer, following the Wellsprings page's wording. The plane pattern breaks, since Salt, the fixed principle, lands on the Fate Plane.

options.label: The doctrine line: Salt reagent, Sulphur Wellspring, Mercury Glyphica
options.consequence: Ties Spagyria to Draft-work and the Standing Index but says nothing about the Crystal. The Necrocursica's residue mapping stays an analogy.

options.label: Furveus's house grammar only, no system link
options.consequence: No new canon. Spagyria is read in Alchemetrica's terms as a Parting, a purification and a Wedding; the Tria Prima stays his personal vocabulary.

questions.rec_reason: The crucible is already a Crystal analogue and the Codex's Emerald Principle is correspondence between scales, so a triad that holds at both scales is the cheapest strong link. Matching by plane keeps it teachable.
questions.evidence: Volume the First 68, 157-158; Necrocursica docx 97-137, 169; Core Vocabulary 55-60; Wellsprings V:22; Alchemetrica 15, 29, 36, 115-117; Heresiology 14.

questions.title: Naming corruptions, and Malphas's charge against Mu-jin
questions.question: Should the texts cite corruptions by name rather than number, and does Malphas keep his charge that Mu-jin's corruption is partly Nomenclature?
questions.context: Volume II's third corruption is Separation Perverted, the Corruption of Non-Commitment ('perfect diagnosis, absent intervention'); Volume III's scholar who describes error 'as though from safety' is the same corruption seen from inside, and the Heresiology orders it third. The Necrocursica's own Third is the Incomplete Sealing, and its Appendix II calls the Codex's Third 'the Cacodaemon of Nomenclature, partially' (Malphas's Sixth), plus an unlisted 'general scholarly Corruption'. Malphas admits Nomenclature in his own early writing.

options.label: Names, not numbers; Appendix II names it, keeps Malphas's charge
options.consequence: Every ordinal becomes a name. Appendix II first calls the Codex's corruption Separation Perverted, then keeps the Nomenclature charge and the 'general scholarly Corruption' paragraph as Malphas's opinion of Mu-jin, not a correction of canon.

options.label: Names, not numbers; cut Appendix II's Nomenclature charge
options.consequence: Appendix II simply names Separation Perverted. The 'general scholarly Corruption' paragraph goes, and with it the only place the two authors argue with each other.

options.label: Keep ordinals, always tagged with the book
options.consequence: 'The Codex's Third', 'the Necrocursica's Third'. Both books stay intact; every reader tracks two numberings and every cross-reference carries a tag.

questions.rec_reason: Malphas concedes Nomenclature in his own early writing, so levelling it at Mu-jin is his voice, not an error. Names end the collision whichever list keeps the 'Seven Cacodaemonic Corruptions' title.
questions.evidence: Heresiology 57-86, 271; Necrocursica 239, 311-333, 469; Vol II docx 235, 265; Vol III docx 30, 234, 382; Codex overview 48.

questions.title: The four corruptions Volume II promised
questions.question: Volume III never delivers the four corruptions Volume II promised it; should the converted Codex give them, and how fully?
questions.context: Volume II lists the remaining four (Conjunction, Fermentation, Distillation and Coagulation Perverted) as 'subjects for the third volume'; Volume III closes without them. Volume II taught the first three from what its author 'recognised in the mirror'. The Heresiology gives all seven, and the Codex overview calls it 'the finished version of a book this man left open', which stays true of a living author. Mu-jin's card: 'He never lets an error stand unspoken.'

options.label: Volume III closes the promise in one paragraph, no case studies
options.consequence: The four by their Heresiology epithets (Instrumental Union, Catastrophic Germination, Sanitized Truth, Tyrannous Finality) and Mu-jin's reason for stopping: he teaches only what he has seen in himself. The promise is kept; the Heresiology stays the finished book.

options.label: Volume III gives all four in full
options.consequence: A short appendix entry per corruption. The Codex is complete, the Heresiology becomes an expansion rather than the completion, and the overview's 'left open' line is rewritten.

options.label: Leave the gap, acknowledged in Volume III
options.consequence: Volume III says the four were left undone. The humility arc stays, the promise stays unkept, and the Heresiology alone supplies the four.

options.label: Cut the promise from Volume II
options.consequence: Removes Volume II's line. The Heresiology's link to the Codex weakens and the overview's 'left open' framing loses its source.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the promise the way Mu-jin's card says he would, the gap named aloud, and follows Volume II's own method of teaching only what he recognised in himself. The Heresiology keeps its role as the finished book.
questions.evidence: Vol II docx 239, 269; Vol III docx 402; Heresiology 57-134; Codex overview 64; Mu-jin's card 118, 137.

questions.title: Reading a corruption on the character sheet
questions.question: Should each corruption leave a readable signature on a character sheet, and through what?
questions.context: Canon ties corruption to the sheet only in general: the Vows are Votia (standing laws the Essence Core adopts), Tempering Coherence (the Crystal's 'internal honesty meter') measures stated law against conduct, a broken vow is a Shear Break (the Core fracturing on a law it was running), and a working 'sustained by refusal' shows as Attunement falling from Coherence. The seven Vows already track the corruptions, but Conviction and Conjunction take two each and Non-Commitment, the Codex's own, none. 'No instrument in the Accord reads grain.'

options.label: Existing instruments only, in general terms
options.consequence: The conversion cites Coherence, the refusal tell and Shear Break without naming which corruption moved them. No table, no new canon; an investigator can see corruption but not which one.

options.label: A stat table per corruption
options.consequence: Each corruption gets the Sub-Stats it moves, the Crystal State it drifts toward and the Stages where it strikes (needs GW1's double seven). New canon, a ratification, and a separate clause for Class Ø practitioners.

options.label: The Vows as signatures; Non-Commitment stays unguarded
options.consequence: The Heresiology states the mapping its Vows imply: each broken vow is its corruption's Shear Break. Non-Commitment reads only as falling Coherence, the one corruption an investigator cannot name from the sheet.

options.label: As C, plus an eighth vow Mu-jin writes
options.consequence: Volume III closes the gap with his vow against his own corruption (in the spirit of 'I will not document what I will not obstruct'), and the Heresiology lists it eighth. Every corruption gets a named, findable counter; grain stays unread.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already says 'the vow is what the soul is failing at'. The one corruption no vow guards is Mu-jin's own, and he already lives under the Dawn Guard's teaching vow, so writing this one is character.
questions.evidence: Heresiology 66-73, 84-86, 99-136, 225-243; Fracture IV:105; Fracture V:198-199; Alchemetrica 82-86, 323-330; Mu-jin's card 27.

questions.title: Where the Codex's Correction sits among theories
questions.question: The Codex ends on 'the Correction': correspondence is a delayed answer, not a mirror. Where does that sit among canon's Four Theories of why a Wellspring answers?
questions.context: The Physical Account gives four accounts of why a Wellspring (one of the sixty laws practitioners draw on) answers: the Consent Doctrine, enforced because it permits licensing; the Correspondence Position ('the same law expressed at two scales'); the Debt Position ('answers on credit', held mostly in the eastern quarter); the Residue Position. None is refuted. The Correction, thesis of all three volumes, makes correspondence 'a law of response', answered 'with delay': the only offered account of how a working could move Tempus, a body in the sky.

options.label: Mu-jin's amendment to the Correspondence Position
options.consequence: One contested school. No system page changes; the Accord keeps enforcing Consent, and Lore & History's line that the formal literature 'does not contain' the Correction stays true.

options.label: Mu-jin's eastern merger of Correspondence and Debt
options.consequence: The answer comes late because it is given on credit and settled out of sight. Still a contested position; the Physical Account gains one line naming it, joining the Aphorism's debt reading and the Tempus drift.

options.label: Canon law: how Wellsprings actually answer
options.consequence: Contradicts the Physical Account's refusal to call the other three refuted, and forces rewrites of Vocatia's definition, the Veil's residue theory and the Accord's licensing basis.

options.label: Cut the Correction
options.consequence: The Codex loses its thesis, the overview's Correction section goes, and the Tempus drift needs another explanation.

questions.rec_reason: It is Mu-jin's own ground: an eastern-adjacent line, and at Rimward he asked without standing and something answered that he cannot shape. The Debt Position explains that; the Correction stays a school, not closed law.
questions.evidence: Physical Account 38-43; Codex overview 68-77; Lore & History 24; Mu-jin's card 25, 163, 178; Tier Ladders X:120; R48-17.

questions.title: Origin of the Aphorism of Mortalis
questions.question: Which text is the Aphorism of Mortalis, the old doctrine of a debt owed to Mortalis or 'He summons himself', and who wrote each?
questions.context: Volume I gives the Aphorism as an old doctrine of the necromantic tradition: the practitioner is 'a debtor who had taken a loan from the Wellspring of Mortalis' (the Wellspring of death). Volume II has the narrator's uncirculated paper gloss it: 'He summons himself, arranged in their image.' Volume III ('which I wrote in the second volume'), the Corrant Papers ('Vis Trismegistus wrote that') and the Codex overview then treat the gloss as the Aphorism itself. The Heresiology's Mortalis row agrees with the gloss: 'The trace is not the soul.'

options.label: Old debt doctrine, with Mu-jin's gloss as his own
options.consequence: Volume II stands as written. Volume III's line becomes 'my gloss of the Aphorism', the Papers' author credits Mu-jin's gloss, and the overview prints doctrine and gloss apart. The debt reading stays for the alchemy-cost rewrite.

options.label: The gloss is the Aphorism, and Mu-jin coined it
options.consequence: Volume I's debt passage and appendix are rewritten to foreshadow Mu-jin's sentence. The debt idea leaves the texts.

options.label: Both are old doctrine; Mu-jin wrote neither
options.consequence: The gloss becomes quoted tradition. Strike Volume II's 'I wrote this down once', Volume III's 'which I wrote' and the Papers' attribution line. Mu-jin loses his one quotable sentence.

questions.rec_reason: Volume II already reads this way, so it costs three small edits. It keeps the debt reading, which suits the Fracture of Worlds cost model and feeds the Debt Position if the Correction takes that route.
questions.evidence: Vol I (vault) 43, 88; Vol II docx 33; Vol III docx 24; Corrant Papers 179-181; Codex overview 55; Heresiology 170.

sections.title: Glyphs, Crafts and operations
sections.intro: The Necrocursica's glyph chains, measured against the Master Glyph Index, the five Crafts and Mechanica.

questions.title: Which glyph names Mu-jin and Malphas write
questions.question: Chains must use Index names; should Mu-jin's prose also mention his older teaching names, and are his Book of Summons and the phoneme table brought into line?
questions.context: Glyphs are written Parun, the language workings are cast in. Rule R18-4 already binds every chain, inscription and chant to the Master Glyph Index (136 forms: Ie Perception, Ma Recall, Wy Motion). The Spirit Rune Arts phoneme table uses older names (Ie Insight, Ma Memory, Wy Truth) and codes the Index lacks (Ci, Zo, No, Ky); Mu-jin's Book of Summons follows it, plus a 'Th Structure' matching neither. Canon has drift precedents: a glyph that 'drifted in meaning', and Law III, a struck error older practitioners still teach.

options.label: Index names only; rewrite the Book of Summons and phoneme table
options.consequence: No old name survives anywhere. Codex and summons page agree; the phoneme table loses the codes the Index lacks (Ci, Zo, No, Tar, Ky, Si, Zu, Fi), and Mu-jin's schooling leaves no trace in his vocabulary.

options.label: Index names in chains; Mu-jin glosses his teachers' names in prose
options.consequence: 'Ie, Perception; I was taught Insight', once per glyph he explains. The Book of Summons' glyph lines move to Index names; the phoneme table stays, labelled an older teaching register that drifted. Malphas writes Index names only.

options.label: Index names in the texts; other pages left as they are
options.consequence: The Codex never mentions the older register. The Book of Summons keeps glyph lines that break R18-4, logged in CONFLICTS.md, and readers meet two names for one glyph with no explanation.

questions.rec_reason: Mu-jin 'never lets an error stand unspoken', and canon already has teachers carrying struck errors, so naming the drift is his voice. Malphas's formula ('Do not improvise it') speaks only the binding names.
questions.evidence: Spirit Rune Arts 100-107; Book of Summons 44, 57, 125; Bench of Attribution 120; Four Crafts, Settled II; R18-4 (pack-18 187-195); Mu-jin's card 137.

questions.title: The Category One seal ending on Fixatio
questions.question: Malphas's forensic seal ends 'Flx (Flux) to Fixatio', but Fixatio is a Wellspring, not a glyph. How should the last step read?
questions.context: Category One is the Necrocursica's authorised death-scene reading: Ie Perception authorises, a five-metre Boundary, Ur Balance directs, then the Sealing chain. Its Ie-Ur-Flx triple is Alchemetrica's own Distillation chain. A glyph is 'a boundary condition imposed on' a law, so a Wellspring cannot be one. Canon names a seal by its Wellspring ('a Fixatio Seal'; 'Fixatio chains close the Draft'). Tp Topology is the only Index form whose primary Wellspring is Fixatio, and the archive already has 'Flux frozen by Topology'.

options.label: 'Flx (Flux), closed on a Fixatio chain'
options.consequence: Canon's own role-by-Wellspring idiom and the smallest change. The seal names one glyph, so the chain cannot be checked past Flux.

options.label: 'Flx (Flux) to Tp (Topology)'
options.consequence: A fully named, checkable chain with an archived precedent. Drops the Wellspring, so the reader loses why this seal holds.

options.label: 'Flx (Flux), sealed by Tp (Topology) on a Fixatio chain'
options.consequence: Names the checkable glyph and the law it runs under in one clause. Topology 'freezes a local outcome grid for a brief window', which suits a field meant to fade cleanly.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps Malphas's 'do not improvise it' formula exact and checkable, uses the Spirit Rune Arts idiom, and matches how Flux has already been sealed in the archive.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 165; Master Glyph Index page 20; Spirit Rune Arts 50, 84; Alchemetrica 102, 121; workbook Tp row; archived scene 20, line 194.

questions.title: The last glyph of the Category Three seal
questions.question: The Category Three seal 'ends with Mortalis itself'. Which glyph closes it and keeps the impression-body (the animated echo built from residue) temporary?
questions.context: A glyph 'creates nothing and carries no power', and none of the 136 forms is named Mortalis. Forms attested at Mortalis include Vor (Return: 'recycles Essence; prevents restless dead'), its unclassified synonym Rt, Ob (Obol: guided soul-crossing) and Au (Death: 'ends unrest'). A spoken Seal names 'the condition on which it ends', and the Warrant (the spoken authorising slot) 'ena' means 'by the dead, in the mouth of the living'. Malphas, co-primary in Mortalis, 'is standing in his own'.

options.label: Vor (Return), written as a closing condition
options.consequence: 'The Mortalis seal', closing on Vor: it ends when the Trace's decision is delivered, opened with 'ena' if spelled out. Explains why the Papers' echo ended 'in one breath' after eleven days.

options.label: Rt (Return), the synonym the Continuum cannot classify
options.consequence: An eerie beat: the glyph that keeps the dead temporary is unclassified. Spends some of the weight canon keeps on the thirty unclassified forms, one of which the Long Reading ties to the Moto seat.

options.label: 'Mortalis itself', as Malphas's heterodox claim
options.consequence: A strong voice beat from a writer standing in Mortalis, but the text asserts what canon calls impossible, so the Necrocursica needs a marked dissent.

options.label: A new Mortalis-named form, as Anamnesis has one
options.consequence: Makes the claim literally true, but adds a 137th form against the Index's Standing Note when Vor already fits.

questions.rec_reason: Canon end to end, exact in meaning and checkable, and the closing condition gives the Papers' abrupt ending a mechanism it currently lacks.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 177; Master Glyph Index page 20, 104, 128; Counted Speech 108, 165; Obrenkael card 68; Malphas's card 54; Corrant Papers 147.

questions.title: Which Craft Mu-jin and Malphas practise
questions.question: Canon gives every named practitioner one Craft, and neither card names one. Which Craft do Mu-jin and Malphas practise?
questions.context: The Crafts: Spellcraft (spoken; dissipates on failure), Runecraft (cut or written into a surface; 'misfires continuously'), Draftcraft (poured into a vessel over a scribed Draft-circle; 'traceable through paperwork'), Chantcraft (sung, needs a choir). Canon: 'Every named practitioner gets a craft.' Mu-jin's card: Draft-circle kit, reagent case, Vocatia 'spoken... over an open Draft-circle', and an inborn sense of a Draft's sealing glyphs 'streets away'. Malphas's card: ferments at benches, a stillroom, a cell that bought stock under a member's name.

options.label: Both Draftcraft
options.consequence: Both cards gain a Craft line. Mu-jin's summons are a spoken call over Draft ground; Malphas pours. Their texts write in price, vessel, seal and ledger, and their work is traceable through provenance.

options.label: Mu-jin Draftcraft, Malphas Runecraft
options.consequence: Malphas's work carries the cutter's hand and misfires until broken. Suits a lich's permanence, but nothing on his card shows him cutting.

options.label: Mu-jin Spellcraft, Malphas Draftcraft
options.consequence: Mu-jin, past Stage VII (Refraction), needs no material anchor, so silent casting marks his rank. His card's Draft-circle kit, vessels and seal sense become props rather than his craft.

questions.rec_reason: Both cards already show benches, vessels and Draft-circles. Draftcraft's cost is provenance, so an investigator can trace either man, and Mu-jin's inborn feel for Draft seals becomes his craft's edge.
questions.evidence: Four Crafts 100-198 (198: every named practitioner gets a craft); Alchemetrica 166; Mu-jin's card 82, 98, 127, 164; Malphas's card 127-134.

questions.title: How Category Three is made and fails
questions.question: Is the Category Three impression-body poured, cut or spoken, and does its Mortalis seal fail by being missing or by being unfinished?
questions.context: The Necrocursica's Incomplete Sealing has the seal both 'not properly executed' and 'absent'; the body then draws ambient Essence and grows 'more itself'. Canon on Runecraft: 'An unsealed rune is an open wound... Environmental Essence bleeds into it', the 'leading cause of runic hauntings'. Draftcraft's Sealing closes 'against contamination and post-completion drift'. Spoken work under the sum 'runs and does not stop'; a skipped Seal means no working. Spoken work leaves no author; cut work carries 'the cutter's hand', poured work 'a maker's mark'.

options.label: Draftcraft throughout: poured over a Draft-circle, seal left unfinished
options.consequence: 'Absent' becomes 'unfinished'. The unsealed Draft drifts and takes in ambient Essence. De Raits is traced by maker's mark and stock ledger, and Mu-jin feels the failing seal streets away.

options.label: Poured body, Mortalis seal written or cut (Runecraft)
options.consequence: The failed seal is an unsealed rune: an open wound that ambient pressure completes into a haunting, misfiring until found and broken. Maker's mark and cutter's hand both trace De Raits, who needs both crafts.

options.label: Spellcraft: spoken, the seal short of the sum
options.consequence: The working runs and does not stop, but a spoken working has no author, so the Corrant investigation loses its trail to De Raits.

questions.rec_reason: Canon's unsealed-rune passage is the Third Corruption almost word for word, and the Authorization reading behind the Mirror Trace is inscription doctrine. The poured body keeps Thom's scaling possible; needing two crafts is the operation's real limit.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 173, 239-251; Spirit Rune Arts 23-26, 36, 51; Alchemetrica (the Sealing), 166; Counted Speech 143, 145; Accord Latin 84-86; Four Crafts 128-131, 177.

questions.title: Where the practitioner's will enters Category Three
questions.question: In the Category Three chain, is the practitioner's Attraction Layer taken in at the Authorization, at the Direction, or at both?
questions.context: Category Three is Volitional Trace Completion: finishing a dead person's unexecuted decision through an impression-body. The Necrocursica uses the practitioner's Attraction Layer (the Crystal's layer of bonds and fixation) as the Direction's 'resonance guide'; its First Corruption, the Mirror Trace, is the practitioner's own patterns absorbed into the Trace. For inscribed work, canon has the Continuum read the Attraction Layer at Authorization, 'part of the rune's permanent structure', and requires harmonisation with the Wellspring invoked: Malphas qualifies for Mortalis, Mu-jin does not.

options.label: Authorization: the Continuum reads the practitioner into the working
options.consequence: One clause moves. The Mirror Trace gets a canon cause at the moment of inscription, and its cure (a third party separating the practitioner's Attraction Layer) stands unchanged.

options.label: Both: read at Authorization, then used again to steer
options.consequence: Two contacts with the Trace. The Mirror Trace becomes likelier and harder to avoid, a heavier cost on every operation, and the text must explain both contacts.

options.label: Direction only, as written
options.consequence: No text change. Holds only if the seal is spoken (GL5 C), since the Authorization reading is inscription doctrine; with a written or cut seal, canon's reading happens anyway and the text leaves it out.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already explains exactly how a practitioner's will gets written into an inscribed working. It costs a clause and keeps the Mirror Trace a risk a careful practitioner can reduce.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 173, 199-213; Spirit Rune Arts 33-36; Core Vocabulary 55-60; Mu-jin's card 48; Malphas's card 53-54.

questions.title: Gravemark Ink for the Category Three seal
questions.question: Should the Category Three seal be written in Gravemark Ink, the Standing Index reagent made for grave-seals?
questions.context: The Standing Index (the Accord's priced catalogue of Drafts and reagents) lists Gravemark Ink at T4, reserved T5, price 31.0. It 'Inscribes a name the Continuum registers', for 'grave-seals that must hold against the thing under them'. Its donor's carry (the donor's essence the ink still holds) 'behaves as though it has an opinion about who is buried', and lawful supply falls short: three sources, and the ink consumes more than they produce. Neither the Necrocursica nor the Codex names a medium for the seal.

options.label: Yes: the lawful formula names Gravemark Ink
options.consequence: Malphas's formula ties to a priced, scarce reagent that suits a written seal. Short or diluted ink becomes a material cause of the Incomplete Sealing, and the supply gap explains where Vaughaus Thom found enough to scale.

options.label: No: the medium stays unnamed
options.consequence: No edits. The Incomplete Sealing keeps only human causes, and Thom's scaling has no material bottleneck.

options.label: Only De Raits uses it, as his signature medium
options.consequence: The formula names no medium; De Raits's bodies carry the ink's registered name, giving the investigation a second trace.

questions.rec_reason: It is canon already, adds real cost and scarcity to the operation, and turns the Incomplete Sealing into something an investigator can assay.
questions.evidence: Standing Index 127; Necrocursica 173-177, 239-245; Corrant Papers 151-155.

questions.title: Mechanica in the Aetheric Bleed
questions.question: Is the Necrocursica's Aetheric Bleed caused by real Mechanica, or by lawful work done badly?
questions.context: Mechanica is forbidden work with no lawful Authorization: it 'always has a donor', who 'may be captive, purchased, dead, or unaware', and it 'cannot end', leaving ground that never heals (Heresiology Grade V). The Fourth Corruption calls its practitioner's work 'legitimate... through sustained Mechanica', files it with the Grade III corruptions, and cures it with months of Wellspring Communion. Its own premise, working 'without adequate Wellspring harmonization', already meets canon's definition: 'A forged authorization is Mechanica by definition.'

options.label: Real Mechanica: Extraction from a dead donor, filed at Grade V
options.consequence: Drop 'legitimate'. The practitioner can be treated over months; the worked ground never heals. The one Mortalis failure that crosses into civilizational breach.

options.label: Lawful but under-harmonised; remove the word Mechanica
options.consequence: Keeps the cure and Grade III. The Bleed comes from repeated over-warranting. Loses the Mechanica link to the magic system.

options.label: Keep the text; note Malphas uses 'Mechanica' loosely
options.consequence: Least rewriting, but a canon term stays misused in a text that faces canon, and every later reader inherits the confusion.

questions.rec_reason: It uses canon's donor and debt mechanics as written. Malphas's own cell had its work closed by the Bureau as 'a bleed with no operator', so he writes this from inside.
questions.evidence: Mechanica page 17-23, 37, 44-50; Heresiology 184-186; Spirit Rune Arts 36; Alchemetrica 277-279; Necrocursica 263-277; Malphas's card 134.

questions.title: Whose Mortalis work is lawfully authorized
questions.question: Which of the texts' operators (Paracelsus, Gillus, Thom) truly hold Mortalis harmonization, so their death-work is lawful rather than forged Mechanica?
questions.context: Canon: an Authorization (the opening glyph that gives a working its warrant) needs real harmonization with the Wellspring, and 'a forged authorization is Mechanica by definition' (unwarranted work that leaves ground permanently open, Heresiology Grade V). Vol III gives Gillus a Stage VII signature with Mortalis primary. Vol II says Paracelsus opened Mortalis 'in the specific, careful manner' of a skilled practitioner. The Necrocursica's Aetheric Bleed is Mortalis work 'without adequate Wellspring harmonization... sustained Mechanica', and Vol III says Thom draws 'with a bucket'.

options.label: Gillus only; Paracelsus and Thom forge it
options.consequence: Both men's Mortalis work is Mechanica with a donor, filed at Grade V. The commission and the Genesio activations become crimes that leave permanent open ground, a far darker Codex and a heavier Papers investigation.

options.label: All three are harmonized; every failure is craft
options.consequence: No forgery anywhere. The Aetheric Bleed needs another cause, and the Necrocursica's Fourth Corruption loses its example in the texts.

options.label: Paracelsus and Gillus harmonized; Thom outruns his at scale
options.consequence: The commission is lawful work done well. Thom's regional scaling tips into Mechanica, giving the Aetheric Bleed its example and the Papers a concrete breach at Genesio.

questions.rec_reason: It matches what each text says of each man, gives the Necrocursica's Fourth Corruption a case inside the story, and keeps the commission lawful, which the Heresiology's Case III treats it as.
questions.evidence: Spirit Rune Arts 36; Vol III docx 50, 136; Vol II docx 223; Necrocursica 265; Heresiology 186 (Grade V)

questions.title: What the Parunic Echo is
questions.question: The Codex calls the Parunic Echo a lasting 'glyph-trace' every advanced practitioner leaves. What is it in current canon terms?
questions.context: Canon says casting's glyphs are 'grammar spoken aloud and then forgotten by the air', so no lasting glyph-trace exists. It does have the Essence Signature, 'the unique trace a practitioner's Essence leaves... You cannot forge one', readable at distance from Stage IV; at Stage X residue holds a practitioner's colour so 'a Mancer arriving a week later can still say who was here'. Aetheric Residue is the change any working leaves on a place. The Corrant Papers rely on 'her Parunic trace'.

options.label: Keep the name; it is the Essence Signature in the Residue
options.consequence: 'Parunic Echo' stays as the trade's word for a practitioner's Essence Signature carried in Aetheric Residue, legible from Stage IV. 'Glyph-trace' goes. Logged as a naming-only extension.

options.label: Drop the coined term for canon's own words
options.consequence: The texts say Essence Signature and Aetheric Residue. Pure canon, but three texts lose a term they lean on.

options.label: The Authorization stamp left by cut or poured work
options.consequence: Grounded in inscription, but spoken workings leave none, so it no longer applies to 'any Temperance-active practitioner'.

options.label: Keep it as written: a lasting glyph-trace
options.consequence: A new canon claim that contradicts 'forgotten by the air' and Mirror-Sign leaving no signature.

questions.rec_reason: The Stage condition the Codex already states matches the Essence Signature's legibility, and the texts keep their word with no new mechanism.
questions.evidence: Core Vocabulary 40, 46; Color of Essence 35, 41; Spirit Rune Arts 23, 36; Descent of Parun 88; Vol II docx 99; Corrant Papers 171.

questions.title: What is written on Jabir's amulet
questions.question: Jabir's copper amulet carries a text in an old Parun hand. What script is it, when every Parun hand is readable by a trained scholar?
questions.context: Volume I: 'a Parunic dialect older than anything catalogued in the Genesio Archivum'; only the overview adds 'a script no Genesio archive could decipher'. Canon: 'There is one script. There have always been fourteen ways to be wrong about that.' Varieties are hands, not dialects, and any Parun sentence is also a working, which fits the resonance Volume I describes. Old High Runic already carries a theorem the Temple of Inscription runs on. Mu-jin, the new recipient, reads glyph chains for a living.

options.label: Very old Old High Runic, readable but undatable
options.consequence: The overview's 'decipher' becomes 'date'. Jabir's recited words are his gloss of the working cut in the copper. Mu-jin reads it at once and cannot place its age.

options.label: Mirror-Sign: a path never cut, unreadable, invisible to wards
options.consequence: Keeps 'undecipherable' and the resonance, but Mirror-Sign is read only by Deepkin, so a Shaneni roadside astrologer carrying it needs a reason.

options.label: Unclassified forms: readable, but the Continuum cannot classify them
options.consequence: A strong mystery for later, but it touches the Long Reading, the claim that the Moto seat's name is written in one of these, which canon keeps deliberately blank.

options.label: A fifteenth, uncatalogued hand
options.consequence: Keeps the overview's wording, but contradicts 'fourteen ways' and needs a canon extension.

questions.rec_reason: Smallest canon footprint, keeps the scene and its resonance, and suits Mu-jin's card: a man of his Perception reads it instantly and fails only to date it. C is the bolder choice.
questions.evidence: Volume the First 96-97; Codex overview 47; Descent of Parun 15, 22, 57-58, 71-74, 85-91; Master Glyph Index page 71-75; Mu-jin's card 57.

questions.title: De Raits's mark on the wax seal
questions.question: What is 'the glyph associated with Gillus De Raits' that the Papers' author recognises on Madeleine Ault's sealed document?
questions.context: The Papers' author saw the mark once before, on a sealed document in the Genesio stacks, and it ties Madeleine Ault's echo to De Raits. Canon: a poured Draft 'carries a maker's mark', read by trace examiners as evidence; an Engraver's mark is 'a signature and a warranty and a legal instrument at once'; a name can be traced as a Parun path; and a Parun instrument doing Aetheric work 'is not a contract but a working'. Check 38 (the glyph-code check) fails unknown bracketed codes.

options.label: His registered craft mark, the one struck on his work
options.consequence: 'Glyph' becomes 'mark': a maker's mark if he pours, an Engraver's mark if he cuts. The same mark sits on his impression-bodies, so the investigator can match the seal to the bodies.

options.label: His name traced as a Parun path, unbracketed
options.consequence: Canon-consistent, unique, passes Check 38. But a letter sealed with a Parun-traced name becomes a working in itself, which the Papers must then account for.

options.label: One of the 136 forms used as his personal mark
options.consequence: Checkable and meaningful (Ma Recall fits his Anamnesis), but a glyph others also use is weak proof of identity.

options.label: A house sigil, not Parun at all
options.consequence: Simplest: 'glyph' becomes 'sigil', and the link to Genesio's sealed stacks stays.

questions.rec_reason: Lower risk than the Parun name and just as unique. It makes the clue a real, findable trace tying the seal to the bodies, which is the investigation's spine.
questions.evidence: Corrant Papers 151-155, 183; The Gate 59; Accord Latin 85, 108; Four Crafts 132; Descent of Parun 206-208; pack-18 394-395.

sections.title: Economy and play
sections.intro: What alchemy costs, who can do it at which rank, and what a player at the table can look up, counter and see coming.

questions.title: What pays for alchemical work
questions.question: When a converted text shows alchemy at work, what pays for it: the stock and the site's vein, the maker's reserve, or both?
questions.context: The texts price nothing. Alchemetrica says a Draft (a preparation holding a working) channels a Wellspring 'through a material medium rather than through their own resonance'; a maker harmonised with that Wellspring causes a quarter of the vein depletion (drain on the channel feeding a site). Pure alchemists (no working Soul Crystal) still make Drafts, and Mu-jin's card prices his Calcination Draft at 'negligible EU' (Essence units). Yet the Tier Ladders charge makers a once-only share of reserve for standing workings: a tenth per blade, a quarter per proofed armour.

options.label: Stock and vein only; the maker pays in time and body
options.consequence: Essence comes from the stock's Provenance (source class) and a draw on the site's vein. Makers pay in hours and in body (crucible palsy, Draft-mark stains), never EU. Fits pure alchemists and Mu-jin's card, but an impression-body costs its maker no reserve.

options.label: Drafts from stock and vein; standing works also cost reserve once
options.consequence: Drafts stay reserve-free. A Crystal-bearer's standing work (a seal, Jabir's amulet, an impression-body) costs a once-only share of reserve on the arms-ladder model; a pure alchemist's needs a Crystal-bearer's seal. Alchemetrica gains one line; Category Three gains a real price.

options.label: The maker's reserve pays a share of every working
options.consequence: Every bench entry carries an EU line. Pure alchemists, having no reserve, cannot work, which breaks Alchemetrica and the Corrant pharmacologist and contradicts 'rather than through their own resonance'.

options.label: As A, with each batch's vein draw measured
options.consequence: Big workings visibly lower a site's rung (its grade on the Tier Ladders), so Genesio carries a measured cost. Needs a draw-per-batch figure canon lacks, derived from the Essence Ledger before use. Makers still pay no reserve.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps Drafts reserve-free as Alchemetrica, pure alchemists and Mu-jin's card require, and extends a live canon precedent so standing works, the impression-body included, carry a cost that hurts.
questions.evidence: Alchemetrica 35, 48, 61, 66, 77; Tier Ladders 147, 509, 560; Mu-jin's card, Calcination Draft row; Standing Index 26.

questions.title: Can a Draft refill a reserve
questions.question: Can a drinkable Draft put Essence back into a practitioner's reserve, the Essence their Soul Crystal holds for working?
questions.context: R2-6, live since Pack Two: 'A practitioner is refilled by a Wellspring, or not at all', because 'Essence cannot be shipped', so 'no consumable restores a practitioner's magazine'; both war pages repeat it. The Tier Ladders' Drafts ladder says what a dose delivers 'is banked there', 'A dose can overfill', and sizes Mnemonis Solution to 'a Stage V reserve'. The Essence Ledger lists 'alchemical treatment' under Active Recovery. The Necrocursica heals a thinned Aether Shell (the Crystal's outer layer) only by months of Wellspring communion.

options.label: R2-6 governs: no Draft refills a reserve
options.consequence: Paracelsus's medicines heal bodies and steady Shells; nothing he brews refuels. The Drafts ladder's 'banked' and 'overfill' sentences and Mnemonis Solution's sizing are corrected. 'Alchemical treatment' reads as speeding Wellspring recovery, not supplying EU.

options.label: The Drafts ladder governs: doses bank EU and can overfill
options.consequence: Philters refuel in the field. R2-6 and The Long March narrow to 'raw Essence cannot be shipped', and Accord logistics, siege arithmetic and every Standing Index consumable are re-read.

options.label: Split: a Draft speeds recovery at rest, never past maximum
options.consequence: Both pages reworded: a Draft shortens Active Recovery, which still means stopping to concentrate, and cannot overfill. Keeps R2-6's battlefield effect, but still puts Essence in a bottle, which R2-6's 'cannot be shipped' denies.

questions.rec_reason: R2-6 is a live design ban restated on both war pages and shapes all logistics. The Necrocursica already obeys it, and Paracelsus as healer of bodies and Shells loses nothing.
questions.evidence: pack-02 R2-6 (222-237); The Long March 37; The War Cycle 41; Tier Ladders 148, 216; Essence Ledger 298; Necrocursica 277.

questions.title: Ranking and capping the Crystal-less alchemist
questions.question: How is a pure alchemist, who has no working Soul Crystal, ranked by the Accord, and what caps the Tier of what they make?
questions.context: Alchemetrica ranks pure alchemists (Class Ø: a Crystal that never woke) 'on the same Tiered Path', with Temperance consulted only above Tier Five, and pictures them 'at Tier Four running the benches that Tier Seven Crystal-bearers put their seals on'. The Tiered Path calls each Tier 'a measurable transformation of the Soul Crystal'; Part Twenty lists Class Ø as pre-Initiate. The Tier Ladders cap an item at the lower of its material's tier and its maker's Tier of Standing (public rank). The Papers' pharmacologist, who reads rooms, fits one.

options.label: Alchemetrica governs: bench-certified Tiers up to Expert cap their work
options.consequence: Pure alchemists hold Tiers of Standing up to Five (Expert) by bench certification, and that Tier caps what they make. The Tiered Path page and Part Twenty gain one carve-out line: bench Tiers are certified, not read off the Crystal.

options.label: No Tier; the sealing Crystal-bearer's Tier caps the work
options.consequence: Pure alchemists rank only on the workshop ladder (Cinderhand to Alchemarch), and their product is capped by whoever seals it, as Alchemetrica already pictures. Its 'same Tiered Path' and 'Tier Four' lines are reworded.

options.label: Keep pure alchemists out of the five texts
options.consequence: No conflict surfaces. The pharmacologist's grain (bench-grown sensitivity no instrument reads) becomes plain intuition, and the Papers lose the one character who shows it.

questions.rec_reason: Alchemetrica is the doctrine R18-5 binds alchemy to, and its built-in injustice, capped at Expert and sealed by Crystal-bearers, is a story engine. One carve-out line squares the Tiered Path.
questions.evidence: Alchemetrica 66, 75-77, 80-86, 308-316; Tiered Path 15; Part Twenty (VIII) 69; Tier Ladders 515; Corrant Papers 43-49.

questions.title: Sub-Stats that govern alchemy and Mortalis work
questions.question: Which Sub-Stats (the sixty-four trained sub-scores under the eight Primaries) govern making a Draft and running a Mortalis operation, on cards and in author notes?
questions.context: Part Fifteen names 'inscribes a Parunic Draft' among the systems the stats govern, then prints profiles for Sage Arts, Summoning, Spirit Rune Arts and Hataraki but none for Drafts. Alchemetrica's three layers (Core, Shell, Attraction Layer) map onto live Sub-Stats, and Harmonics Attunement 'Reduces draw cost'. Mu-jin's Sight Through the Glass already routes Gnosis Analysis through the Attraction Layer. Mortalis (the Wellspring of death and passage) strengthens Resilience Persistence and Gnosis Cognition. R47-10: governing Sub-Stats belong to the practitioner. The in-world prose names no Sub-Stats either way.

options.label: Borrow the Spirit Rune Arts profile whole, plus Harmonics Attunement
options.consequence: No new rule. Gnosis Fluency; Ardency Density, Compression, Depth; Resilience Ward, Hardening; Dexterity Finesse, Tempering Clarity, Dominion Gravity; plus Attunement for draw cost. Ward and Gravity suit standing runes better than a bench.

options.label: A Draft profile built from existing Sub-Stats, filed for ratification
options.consequence: Core to Tempering Coherence and Maturity, Shell to Tempering Clarity, Attraction Layer to Harmonics Attunement; Gnosis Analysis and Fluency for reading and chain; Vitality Filtration for exposure. Mortalis work adds Persistence and Cognition. Filed through propose_rule.

options.label: Keep stats off alchemy
options.consequence: Fastest. Nothing mechanical explains why Paracelsus's precision or Mu-jin's reading matters, and card Draft techniques stay unanchored.

questions.rec_reason: Part Fifteen names Drafts among the stat-governed systems and then skips them. This fills the gap with no new stat and matches the routing Mu-jin's card already uses.
questions.evidence: Part Fifteen (V) 98, 163, 179-183, 199; IV. Sub-Stats 18, 29, 55, 76, 102-105; Alchemetrica 57-61; R47-10; Mu-jin's card, Sight Through the Glass.

questions.title: The missing Real Alchemy page
questions.question: The Real Alchemy, the third alchemy source R18-5 requires, exists nowhere readable. How does the alchemy conversion proceed?
questions.context: R18-5 names three alchemy sources, 'consulted in this order, and none of them optional': the Alchemical Index (what exists), Alchemetrica (doctrine) and The Real Alchemy (the real-world check on invented process, apparatus and reagent behaviour). No page of that name is in the wiki mirror, the true-canon vault or Notion. The conversion's invented processes (spagyric separation, the stabilisation protocol, Paracelsus's metals) are exactly what the page was meant to check.

options.label: Hold the alchemy passes until the page is found
options.consequence: Attribution and setting work carries on; every alchemy passage waits, against the standing rule that nothing waits on Isaac.

options.label: Proceed on Alchemetrica and research
options.consequence: Process claims are checked against Alchemetrica's material sections (vessels, heat, lute, menstrua, bodily costs) and wotr-phenomenon research (the real-physics check). Some risk of divergence if the page surfaces.

options.label: Proceed, and write The Real Alchemy from the conversion's research
options.consequence: As B, and the research gathered (Paracelsus's dosing, spagyric separation, luting, long calcinations) becomes The Real Alchemy page for ratification, so every later alchemy task has R18-5's third source.

questions.rec_reason: Nothing waits, the research has to be done anyway, and later alchemy work gets the source R18-5 requires instead of inheriting the same gap.
questions.evidence: pack-18 R18-5 (234-258); Pack Eighteen source 75; CONFLICTS.md C-058; no Real Alchemy page in wiki, true-canon vault or Notion (2026-09-28).

questions.title: Paracelsus's arsenic and mercury
questions.question: How does the converted Codex present Paracelsus's medicines of arsenic and mercury?
questions.context: Volume I: his use of arsenic and mercury 'was reckless but not incorrect in principle'; the Necrocursica calls him the finest iatrochemist (a physician who treats with prepared minerals) its author knew. Canon names raw minerals plainly (antimony, saltpetre, vitriol) and gives made solvents trade names. Alchemetrica's crucible palsy (a writing-hand tremor, then irritability and shyness) is mercury poisoning in all but name; Draft-mark stains sclera and nailbeds. Cael Dareth's card has 'hands burned pale by mercury'. Arsenic appears nowhere else in canon.

options.label: Real names; the dose is the point; he carries the cost
options.consequence: The medicine heals at a dose and poisons past it. Paracelsus shows early crucible palsy and Draft-mark, which Mu-jin reads on sight. Dose and mechanism are checked by research before print.

options.label: In-world trade names for the metals
options.consequence: Fits the solvent-naming habit (Strongwater, Kingswater). Loses the historical nod and breaks canon's plain naming of raw minerals.

options.label: Cut the iatrochemistry line
options.consequence: Loses the trait that defines him, and the Necrocursica's 'iatrochemist' line needs rewording.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already names raw minerals plainly and has written mercury's symptoms into the trade's cost table, so the line becomes a visible cost Mu-jin can observe, not flavour.
questions.evidence: Volume the First 68, 161; Necrocursica 121; Alchemetrica 72, 212-218, 248-249, 294; Cael Dareth's card 24; no 'arsenic' elsewhere in wiki or rules.

questions.title: How access and clearance are written
questions.question: The texts gate access with numbered 'Accord Level III to VI clearance'. How should access to documents and operations be written instead?
questions.context: Canon has no numbered clearance Levels, and 'Level' is the character Level (1 to 500), so the phrase fails R14-5's exact-terms check. Canon gates people by Tier: Lyssara Veyn, a senior Mortalis scholar, holds 'Clearance Tier II Restricted'. The Bench of Attribution (the formula registry) reserves formulas, 'forbidden to any practitioner below a stated Tier'; the Heresiology classes seized texts (ward, redaction, excerpt, seal-only). The Necrocursica calls itself sealed and restricted; about a dozen lines, Appendix I's included, carry Levels. Whatever you pick applies inside the Guild Accord as it forms now: its rules bind only the circles that have signed (R60-09, R60-18).

options.label: Bench reservation for operations; sealed treatise; Lyssara-style clearance for files
options.consequence: Categories are Bench-reserved by named Tier (EC10 sets which). The Necrocursica is 'sealed' everywhere, as its title page says. The Papers' header and Appendix I read like Lyssara's card ('Tier IV Restricted'). Every Level line changes.

options.label: One Tier clearance scale everywhere, operations included
options.consequence: Matches Lyssara's card wording, but her Tier II Restricted then bars canon's senior Mortalis scholar from Category One unless her card changes.

options.label: Keep Levels as the Division's internal scale, glossed to Tiers
options.consequence: Few edits. Canon gains a second clearance vocabulary needing a canonical home, and nobody can compare Level IV with Tier II.

options.label: Heresiology seizure classes for every document; reservation for operations
options.consequence: The Necrocursica is seal-only and the Papers transmissible only by excerpt. Canon's text machinery throughout, but the Papers are an investigator's working files, not seized texts, so the class misfits them.

questions.rec_reason: Canon has a device for each thing the texts gate: Bench reservation for workings, 'sealed' for the treatise its own title page seals, Lyssara's clearance form for a file. Nothing is invented.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 13, 161, 169, 173, 457, 505; Corrant 5, 281; Lyssara's card 24, 31; Bench of Attribution 86; Standing Index 127; Heresiology 196; I. Levels 16.

questions.title: Where Mortalis costs, floors and counters live
questions.question: Where do the Mortalis Categories' cost, limits, tell, counter and Stage floor live: in the texts' prose, in canon entries, or both?
questions.context: The Necrocursica sets out four Categories of Mortalis (death-and-passage Wellspring) operation: reading residues, stabilising them, Volitional Trace completion (building an impression-body, a likeness of the dead) and forbidden resurrection. Canon has no table for them: two Mortalis formulas in the Alchemical Index, near precedents with floors in the Spell Index, and a Counterplay page silent on alchemy. R57-07 makes in-world documents fully metaphysical; R47-2 sets the field format for ability entries; fair-play says documents give pieces, not solutions.

options.label: Both: pieces in the prose, a field-format entry per Category
options.consequence: The texts carry law, cost and tell in each author's voice. Categories One to Three each get an R47-2 entry and a Spell Index row with a Stage floor; Category Four gets a refusal entry. Every counter can be looked up.

options.label: Spell Index rows only; the texts stay lore
options.consequence: Citable floors and glyphs, but the documents carry no metaphysics, which breaks R57-07.

options.label: Author notes mapping each Category to a precedent
options.consequence: Fastest. Category Three stays uncosted and players cannot find its counters.

options.label: Texts only, no canon entries
options.consequence: Satisfies R57-07, but nothing can be looked up, failing fair-play's findable-counter rule.

questions.rec_reason: Only this satisfies R57-07 and fair-play together, and the Spell Index already holds precedent rows (Equilibrium Archive, Sediment Reading, The Still Gate's Mercy) to set floors against.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 161-181; Codex Alchemical Index #16, #27; Spell Index rows 9, 10, 32, 42, 86, 95, 98; Counterplay 15-66; R57-07; R47-2; fair-play 44-70.

questions.title: What a Mortalis or Anamnesis working costs
questions.question: What does each Mortalis Category, the impression-body and the Genesio activation actually pay, in canon's own currencies?
questions.context: The texts price nothing. Canon already has every piece: a share of the maker's reserve for standing works, depletion of the site ('the room pays'), waste radiating as heat (R47-8), the Veil's Drift Scale (how far a threshold has been worn), and Anamnesis's inherited failure, which erases what it reads. EC8 decides where these costs are written down; this decides what they are.

options.label: The full stack, and a Trace can be used once
options.consequence: Reserve share, site depletion, waste heat, a Drift Scale tick for Category Two and up, and every Anamnesis read erasing what it takes. The Genesio activation gets a hard limit and a visible scar.

options.label: The same stack without the Veil drift
options.consequence: Lighter bookkeeping; the Codex's long crossing of the Veil costs nothing measurable.

options.label: Reserve share and site depletion only
options.consequence: Simplest to run at the table, but Anamnesis reads become repeatable and the Genesio activation has no natural stop.

questions.rec_reason: Every piece is already canon, the costs hurt and can be seen, and a once-only Trace gives the Genesio story its own brake.
questions.evidence: The Veil 76, 89; Essence Ledger 266, 298; R47-8, R47-9, R47-11; Limina 66; X. Tier Ladders 482

questions.title: Stage floor for each Mortalis Category
questions.question: What minimum Temperance Stage (the practitioner's measured degree of soul refinement) does each Mortalis Category require?
questions.context: The texts gate Categories One, Two and Three at 'Level III, IV and V'. Read as Tiers of Standing those are Journeyman (Stage III), Adept (IV) and Expert (Stages V to VII). The Spell Index's nearest precedents sit higher: Equilibrium Archive and Obol Passage at Flourishing (IV), Sediment Reading and Soul-Drift Passage at Glory (VI), The Still Gate's Mercy (letting the dying pass without leaving an Echo) at Transcendence (VIII). Gillus, the Category Three operator, is Stage VII (Refraction), where the Necrocursica says the Continuum starts presenting Traces as tasks.

options.label: The texts' numbers read straight: Ascension, Flourishing, Splintering
options.consequence: Fewest changes. Category One sits at Journeyman, below Equilibrium Archive and Sediment Reading, so reading the dead becomes ordinary trade work.

options.label: Flourishing, Glory, then Refraction with individual review
options.consequence: Categories One and Two sit on precedent rows; Category Three sits where the Necrocursica says Trace-compulsion begins. Gillus stands at the floor, lawful by rank and unlawful only by review. Reservations read Adept, Expert, Expert with review.

options.label: Higher: Category Three at Transcendence, after The Still Gate's Mercy
options.consequence: Gillus falls below the floor, so his completions are unlawful by rank as well as review, and Thom's replication at scale needs a Master-rank operator or a stated shortcut.

questions.rec_reason: One and Two rest on existing Spell Index rows, Category One stays professional work, and Category Three's floor is the Stage where the Necrocursica itself says the pull to complete Traces begins.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 161, 169, 173, 345; II. Grades 64-79; Spell Index rows 10, 32, 86, 95, 98; Volume III 50 (Gillus at Stage VII).

questions.title: The impression-body's tells and counters
questions.question: Beyond canon's general counters, what gives an impression-body away, and what can end one early?
questions.context: An impression-body is the texts' built likeness of a dead person, completed from their Volitional Trace (the residue of their will). Canon's general counters: wasted energy radiates as heat (R47-8); a drawn site stays thinner, 'the tell and also the counter'; workings inherit their Wellsprings' failures, which opponents can induce (R47-9), and Anamnesis (the memory Wellspring) erases what it reads. Stillgate Ash, a Mortalis powder, gives the dead's residual field 'a path to earth'. The Heresiology: 'The trace is not the soul.'

options.label: Canon's general counters only
options.consequence: Heat, the thinned site and induced Anamnesis erasure. No new mechanics. The body itself is undetectable; only its making leaves a trail.

options.label: General counters plus a Trace-without-Crystal tell
options.consequence: A Category One reading (Distillation, the forensic operation) finds identity-shaped carry (material that holds a person's pattern) with no Soul Crystal behind it. A trained reader within reach can tell likeness from person; the mourner still cannot, as Heresiology Case III shows.

options.label: As B, plus Stillgate Ash as the material counter
options.consequence: A ring of Stillgate Ash (Journeyman gate) grounds the body's residual charge and lets it complete its passage. Living Essence at the ring bleeds too, so the counter costs whoever uses it.

questions.rec_reason: Every piece is canon or read straight from it: a tell a trained reader (Mu-jin, harmonised with Distillation, among them) can find, a counter a quartermaster can buy, and a price for using it.
questions.evidence: R47-8, R47-9; Essence Ledger 266; The Veil 60, 76; Alchemical Index 46 (Stillgate Ash); Heresiology 170, 209; Alchemetrica 29, 102; Mu-jin's card 48.

questions.title: What kind of commission Paracelsus took
questions.question: What kind of transaction was Paracelsus's commission for the grieving nobleman, and did money change hands?
questions.context: In canon a Commission is an Accord instrument with a Danger Tier and a Sigil. The Heresiology uses the private sense ('The Eastern Commission of Grief', 'grief-powered commissions'). Alchemetrica: unentered formulas (never registered with the Bench of Attribution) are 'lawful to hold and unlawful to sell'. The Corrant Papers tell the patron that 'commissioning a practitioner is not itself a clear violation'. The texts never mention a fee. Whether the working was paid decides whether Paracelsus broke the law and whether the investigator has an enforcement hook.

options.label: Private, unentered and paid: he sold what he could only hold
options.consequence: The patron broke no law, so the Papers' line stands as said to him; Paracelsus carries the breach and a Master of the Circle's personal liability (the rank that seals). The Codex names the fee; the Papers author has a case.

options.label: Private and unpaid: a favour, lawful to hold and perform
options.consequence: No one broke the Bench's law; only the Heresiology's Mortalis doctrine condemns it. The Papers' line stands, and the investigator has a doctrinal hook but no legal one.

options.label: An Accord Commission with Danger Tier and Sigil
options.consequence: The Accord sanctioned it, which contradicts the Codex's secrecy and the Heresiology's Mortalis doctrine.

options.label: Rename it an 'engagement'
options.consequence: Avoids the collision and breaks the link to Heresiology Case III's title.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps every existing line true: the Papers speak to the patron, the Heresiology's private sense holds, and Paracelsus pays a real legal cost the investigator can find and press.
questions.evidence: Tier Ladders 56-71; Alchemetrica 302, 308-316; Bench of Attribution 49; Heresiology 170, 210; Volume II 23, 121-123; Corrant Papers 125.

questions.title: How many figures the prose carries
questions.question: How many measured figures (EU, AU/s, η) does each converted document state in its own prose?
questions.context: The five texts give no numbers. R57-07 makes every in-world document fully metaphysical; R48-16 says anyone with an instrument or trained eye 'states figures as often as they would'. EU is Essence units, AU/s the output rate, η efficiency. Mu-jin's card carries his own EU, AU/s and η, and his signature Sight Through the Glass gives a full diagnostic overlay. R47-4 says costs are shares of reserve read off the Essence Ledger's bands for the Stage, so no figure may be invented.

options.label: Each author states figures as their instruments give them
options.consequence: Mu-jin reads EU, η and site density whenever he removes his spectacles; Malphas prices each Category as a share of reserve by Stage; the investigator logs readings at scenes. The impression-body's cost, Genesio's density and the drift's scale are derived.

options.label: Figures in the Necrocursica only
options.consequence: The memoir and field notes stay literary and the treatise carries the numbers. Reads naturally, but the Codex falls short of R57-07 and Mu-jin under-uses his own signature instrument.

options.label: Figures only in companion entries
options.consequence: The documents stay number-free, contradicting R57-07 and R48-16.

questions.rec_reason: It is what the rules say, it fits each author's instrument and voice, and it forces the missing numbers to be derived from the Ledger instead of guessed.
questions.evidence: R57-07; R48-16; R47-4; Mu-jin's card 75-76, 96; fair-play 13-18; the five texts carry no figures.

questions.title: How much procedure the Necrocursica gives
questions.question: How complete are the Necrocursica's working procedures in the copy the reader holds, and what fills its empty Appendix I?
questions.context: Chapter the Second, 'A Practitioner's Compendium', gives full glyph chains (Authorization to Sealing) for Categories One to Three. Appendix I, the Stabilization Protocol credited to Paracelsus and the author, holds only a pointer to a Technical Supplement: 'good luck, they are very slow'. Heresiology Case II calls the manuscript 'technically brilliant but spiritually dangerous', a weaponised text. Its seizure classes include 'preservable under redaction'. Fair-play says documents give 'pieces, not solutions'; R47-1 says entries never tell the reader how to use a working.

options.label: Full chains everywhere; Appendix I stays a pointer
options.consequence: The treatise is a working recipe for impression-bodies. Case II holds literally, but the challenge of piecing Category Three together is gone.

options.label: Law, roles, cost; Category Three's completion withheld; Appendix I sealed
options.consequence: Categories One and Two keep their chains. The missing Supplement becomes an in-world objective, findable in the Accord archive or on a marginal-note copy.

options.label: The Accord's redacted copy: completion struck, Appendix I printed
options.consequence: The sealed original stays complete, so Case II holds. The reader's copy has Category Three's completion steps struck under 'preservable under redaction', and the stabilisation protocol, the defensive counter to a failing seal, printed in full.

options.label: Full chains and full Appendix I
options.consequence: A complete manual, attack and defence, with nothing left to find.

questions.rec_reason: Case II's weaponised original stays true, the reader gets pieces rather than a recipe, and the printed protocol is exactly the findable defensive counter fair-play asks for.
questions.evidence: Necrocursica 13, 155-186, 455-457; Heresiology 196, 208; fair-play 67-69; R47-1; R47-3; Alchemetrica 102.

questions.title: Naming the Castlefall circle's ink
questions.question: Should the Papers' unnamed Mortalis ink on the Castlefall circle become a canon formula, and when does the investigator name it?
questions.context: The Papers: the circle in the tanner's flat 'was drawn in an ink that catches the light differently', like 'materials associated with Mortalis-adjacent practice'; the investigator is 'very carefully not drawing conclusions' and sends a floor sample to Genesio. Canon's Gravetide Ink (Mortalis) is 'the Boundary role made material' for contracts with the dead: where they reach and when they end. Stillgate Ash, canon's only circle-drawn Mortalis material, is a powder that grounds the dead's residual field.

options.label: Gravetide Ink, named in that entry
options.consequence: One canon formula anchors the scene, and the investigator's caution line is cut.

options.label: Gravetide Ink, named when the Genesio analysis returns
options.consequence: Keeps the caution beat. A later entry names it from the sample, giving the reader a findable piece and tying the circle to the Boundary role. The circle is the Boundary (Gravetide Ink); the Category Three seal is the Sealing (Gravemark Ink, GL7): two glyph roles on one site.

options.label: Stillgate Ash, with 'ink' rewritten as a drawn powder line
options.consequence: The circle becomes a grounding ring rather than a contract with the dead, which suits a clean-up and blurs the scene's evidence of a completion.

options.label: Leave it unnamed
options.consequence: No change; the ink stays flavour.

questions.rec_reason: Gravetide Ink's canon job, stating when a working on the dead ends, is what a Category Three circle needs, and naming it late keeps the investigator's caution and the fair-play piece.
questions.evidence: Corrant Papers 51-53; Alchemical Index 46, 68; Codex Alchemical Index #16, #27.

sections.title: Setting
sections.intro: Where the texts happen: places, institutions and the sky, most of which canon does not have yet.

questions.title: Where the Trans-Alftian region sits
questions.question: Where on the canon map do the Codex's places (the terraces, Castlefall, Genesio, Urbis, the eastern lowlands) sit, now that Mu-jin walks them?
questions.context: None of these places exists outside the texts, and canon's 'east' is a whole quarter, the New World. Mu-jin's card has him born to the Mahuo court line at Sum-gol; the Ketsuen page puts Sum-gol in that Inner World state, which runs 'from the northeastern shield's limestone valleys', with river-valley farming, Uplands herbs 'alchemists value' and its densest natural seeps. The Inner World is the Concord heartland; its Stillband iron is 'the backbone of every bridge and rail in the quarter'.

options.label: Inner World: Ketsuen's valleys and Uplands, toward the Concord heartland
options.consequence: The terraces become Ketsuen's limestone valleys, Genesio sits among the Uplands' dense seeps, Castlefall is a valley rail town and Urbis a heartland city. Invented names survive, including Heresiology Case IV. One geography note on the Ketsuen page.

options.label: Replace them with canon places: Sum-gol, the Uplands, Nalūn
options.consequence: Fewest new places, but Heresiology Case IV ('The Genesio Activation Sequence') and dozens of lines are renamed.

options.label: A separate invented region off the mapped kingdoms
options.consequence: Least rewriting; adds unplaced geography and pulls Mu-jin far from Sum-gol, Rimward and the Ashgate road on his card.

questions.rec_reason: Ketsuen already has the limestone valleys, alchemists' herbs, dense seeps and rail iron the texts need, and it keeps Mu-jin on the ground his card walks without inventing a new corner of the world.
questions.evidence: Ketsuen page 20, 68-72; Mu-jin's card 25, 162; Modern Era 41; Inner World (Bearing and Holding) 47; Four Quarters 25; Heresiology 211.

questions.title: Where Jabir's Shaneni empire lies
questions.question: Is the Shaneni empire, whose borders Jabir came from, a new polity or a place canon already has?
questions.context: Volume I: Jabir 'had come from the Shaneni empire's borders', and his knowledge 'was a synthesis of traditions most scholars treated as incompatible'; his eastern tradition is half the Codex's Hermetic synthesis. 'Shaneni' is nowhere in canon. Canon's east is the New World, where Eresse, a living elven principality, keeps 'Four Eons of Eressean law' on the old-ground beside the chartered arc, and the two legal orders fight over titles. Mu-jin's card calls his own line 'Eastern Concord-adjacent'.

options.label: A new living empire in the east
options.consequence: Adds a polity that the Powers of the Imperial Age page and the map must carry.

options.label: The New World border where Eresse's old-ground meets the chartered arc
options.consequence: No new polity. 'The Shaneni empire's borders' becomes that border, where two incompatible orders share ground, which explains his synthesis. One line reworded; nothing added to Eresse's page.

options.label: The Concord east, Mu-jin's own lineage ground
options.consequence: Makes the eastern tradition part of Mu-jin's inheritance, but ties it to his unsettled 'Eastern Concord-adjacent' origin.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already has a border where two incompatible orders share ground, which is exactly what the texts say Jabir's learning is, and nothing is added to the map.
questions.evidence: Volume the First 93; Powers of the Imperial Age 88-96, 285; Four Quarters 25; Mu-jin's card 25; no 'Shaneni' in canon.

questions.title: What Genesio is, and how far
questions.question: Is Genesio one place or two, and how far is it from Castlefall, by what route?
questions.context: Volume I makes Genesio a town with streets, a craft district and 'the largest' Archivum, with the friends' flat above a tanner's workshop nearby. Volume III calls it a 'mountain territory, three days' travel from Castlefall'; the Papers put it 'four hundred kilometres north'; the Necrocursica has a platform at 'a Genesio waystation'. R53-08's rates: mounted 30 to 40 miles a day, less in passes, rail where it runs. 400 km, about 250 miles, is six to eight days mounted or under a day by rail.

options.label: One mountain territory: rail to a railhead, then the passes
options.consequence: A day by rail to the Genesio waystation, then two days mounted up the passes: both figures hold. Its archive-town holds the Archivum. Volume I's tanner's flat moves to Castlefall, where Volume II and the Papers already put it.

options.label: One place, three days mounted, no rail
options.consequence: About 100 to 120 miles. 'Four hundred kilometres' is cut from the Papers and the Necrocursica's Genesio platform goes.

options.label: Rail all the way, under a day
options.consequence: 'Three days' travel' is cut; Genesio becomes a rail town and loses its remoteness.

options.label: Two places: a town near the terraces and a mountain territory
options.consequence: Every 'Genesio' line must say which one, and readers will conflate them.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps every figure the texts give, matches canon's rule that provincial rail stops at the county town, and fits the Heresiology's single Genesio case.
questions.evidence: Volume I (vault) 13, 18, 27; Volume III 174; Corrant 37-43, 205; Necrocursica 365; R53-08; Works and Days 259; Heresiology 211.

questions.title: One or two Archivums; where the Monastery stands
questions.question: How many Herald Archivums are there, and where does the Monastery stand?
questions.context: Volume I reads at 'the Archivum in Genesio', yet is filed from 'the Archivum of the Heralds, Urbis'. Volume II is recovered from 'the lower Archive of the Herald's Monastery, Urbis', then 'the sealed lower stacks of the Herald's Archivum, Urbis'. The Papers cite Genesio's lower stacks. The Necrocursica's author is confined at 'the Genesio Monastery'. Volume I reaches the Monastery by a snowy high road from Castlefall and a humming Heraldic bridge; Volume II rides home from it to Castlefall.

options.label: Two Archivums; the Monastery at Urbis houses the Urbis Archivum
options.consequence: Genesio's is the older outlying house with its own sealed stacks; Urbis's sits in the Monastery's lower floors, so Volume II's two lines already agree. Only the Necrocursica's 'Genesio Monastery' changes.

options.label: Two Archivums; the Monastery alone on the high road
options.consequence: Volume II's 'Herald's Monastery, Urbis' becomes 'Herald's Archivum, Urbis', the Necrocursica's line changes, and the Monastery needs its own place on the map.

options.label: One Archivum, at Genesio
options.consequence: Every Urbis filing line moves, including Volume I's header, Volume II's colophon and Gillus's letter address.

options.label: The Monastery at Genesio, as the Necrocursica says
options.consequence: Volume I's ride and Volume II's return to Castlefall become 250-mile journeys.

questions.rec_reason: It turns Volume II's apparent contradiction into one building, suits the humming bridge and Urbis's Heraldic spires, and costs a single edit.
questions.evidence: Volume I (vault) 13, 46, 53; Volume the First 14; Volume II 5, 19, 282; Corrant 69; Necrocursica 5; Volume III 404, 406.

questions.title: What the Heralds are
questions.question: What are the Heralds, the body that runs the Archivums, the Monastery, the Medical University and the humming bridges?
questions.context: No Herald order exists in canon. An Archon (one of the Fourteen ruling cosmic principles) 'has a seat, a court, a lineage of heralds'. Maelor, Archon of Memory, 'governs all acts of remembrance, recording, echo transcription, and soul lineage tracking'. Auren, Archon of Death, has a living herald, Vaerath Ashveil, 'Herald of Auren. Death-Speaker'. The Heresiology expects Monasteries that 'Teach the Great Work as discipline before technique' but names none. The Codex's Heralds keep archives, teach, heal and build humming stone.

options.label: A new Hermetic teaching order, older than the Accord's communion
options.consequence: One Factions page. Fills the Heresiology's unnamed Monasteries and keeps the monks, Prior and Sacred Discourse as written, with no tie to the cosmology.

options.label: An order grown from Maelor's lineage of heralds
options.consequence: One Factions page and a line on Maelor's page. The Archivums, the Silent Archivists and the Genesio Anamnesis site gain a patron whose office is memory; Asclepius's scorn for 'God-Essence' becomes a quarrel with the order's theology.

options.label: An order grown from Auren's lineage of heralds
options.consequence: Ties the Mortalis-heavy texts to Vaerath Ashveil's live card, which must take the order into her history; archives and medicine fit Death less well.

options.label: Fold them into the Accord's academies
options.consequence: No new order. The Medical University becomes a chartered academy (Scholar to Chair), but the Monastery and bridges need another owner.

questions.rec_reason: Memory is what the Heralds do in every text: archives, transcription, the Anamnesis site. Maelor's canon office matches it, and the order still fills the Heresiology's monastery duty.
questions.evidence: Fourteen Titans 20; Pair II (Maelor) 27; Fourteen Archons 100, 108; Vaerath Ashveil's card 24; Heresiology 218; Modern Era 112-116; Volume the First 59, 102, 122.

questions.title: What Urbis is
questions.question: What is Urbis, where the Papers address the Research and Archives Division and the Heralds keep their seat?
questions.context: Urbis is not in canon. The Research and Archives Division's instrument, the Archives Eternal, is sealed 'beneath the Council Spire of the Concord Citadel', and the Citadel is 'a nexus suspended between planes'. The Inner World is the Concord heartland, with 'the chancery schools, the conduit network at its densest'. The texts give Urbis a railway, Heraldic spires, a Medical University and city-states 'in the Urbis orbit'.

options.label: A new Inner World heartland city with a regional Division office
options.consequence: The Archives Eternal stays at the Citadel; the Papers' address is a regional desk. One line of geography; rail and trams suit a heartland city.

options.label: The city below the Concord Citadel
options.consequence: The Papers become Citadel documents, but a railway into a between-planes nexus needs new invention.

options.label: Replace Urbis with Stannvaard, the Guild Seat, or an Altherion city
options.consequence: No new city. The Heraldic spires, Medical University and Monastery move there and must fit that place's existing page.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the Papers' address and the Heralds' seat working with no new metaphysics, and the heartland already has the rail, schools and conduit density the texts describe.
questions.evidence: Concordance 14; Modern Era 41, 53; Concord Citadel 15; Corrant 231; Volume the First 130; Volume II 249.

questions.title: Naln: Nalūn or somewhere else
questions.question: Is 'Naln', home of the Silent Archivists and an Accord observation post, the canon kingdom Nalūn with its diacritic lost?
questions.context: The volumes are 'Transcribed by the Silent Archivists of Naln'; the Papers verify the Tempus drift at 'the Accord's own observation post at Naln'. Canon's Nalūn is an Inner World salt kingdom beside Ketsuen, on Mu-jin's road (Rimward is its eastern frontier city). Its Vaultmere is 'the counting city' of archivists and sealed chambers; its Deepvein holds a Measurewright station that measures contracts. Both profiles are marked pending ratification. The Measurewrights (canon's assayers and instrument-keepers) hold the Bench's instrument chair.

options.label: Nalūn: Vaultmere's archivists transcribe; the Measurewrights verify the drift
options.consequence: Two orphans tie to canon, and Vaultmere's pending archivist profile goes into use and needs ratifying. The 'observation post at Naln' becomes the Measurewrights' instrument chair, since Deepvein measures contracts, not skies.

options.label: Nalūn for both, with a new sky-watching post there
options.consequence: Keeps the Papers' line, but adds a station Nalūn's page lacks, in a kingdom cut into an underground salt basin.

options.label: A separate new place called Naln
options.consequence: One letter from a canon kingdom; readers will take it for a typo.

options.label: Cut Naln
options.consequence: The Research and Archives Division transcribes and the Measurewrights verify; the colophon loses its texture.

questions.rec_reason: The name is Nalūn's, Vaultmere already does the archivists' job, and the Measurewrights are canon's instrument authority, so every role lands on something that exists.
questions.evidence: Nalūn page 22, 48, 50, 159; Natsume Kurogiku's card 139; Bench of Attribution 35; Lore & History 33; Corrant 25; Volume II 281.

questions.title: What Tempus is in the canon sky
questions.question: Which body in the canon sky is Tempus, the texts' 'great gas-giant' whose drift carries their argument?
questions.context: Volume II calls Tempus 'our great gas-giant, that patient eye in the night sky' and sees it by day. Canon's sky is 'One sun. One moon. Five wanderers', with nothing giant by day. The Weight (Moto name Omomi) circles in about twenty-nine years and is used for 'Generational reckoning'; the Lantern (Akari) takes about twelve. Those are Saturn's and Jupiter's periods, and real alchemy made Saturn the planet of time and lead. Heresiology Case V is 'The Drift of Tempus'.

options.label: The Hermetic name for the Weight, the 29-year wanderer
options.consequence: Fits five wanderers: Tempus means time and the Weight counts generations, so its drift is a public shock. The daylight-eye image goes; Case V keeps its name.

options.label: The Hermetic name for the Lantern, the 12-year wanderer
options.consequence: Same edits. Its real analogue is the larger giant, but the name loses its link to generational time.

options.label: A sixth body, visible by day
options.consequence: Keeps the image; the Sky page's opening line and every sky scene are rewritten.

options.label: The Sower's drift instead
options.consequence: Joins canon's existing calendar quarrel, but contradicts the arithmetic cause canon already gives that drift.

questions.rec_reason: It fits the canon sky, the name already means what the Weight is used for, and the Weight's circuit is Saturn's, the planet real alchemy tied to time.
questions.evidence: Volume II 213, 243; Volume III 310; Sky, the Hour and the Year 17, 29-30, 128-129; Heresiology 212; Lore & History 42.
